title: Man'oushe Za'atar
summary: Lebanon's morning flatbread, a soft yeasted dough stretched thin, dimpled and painted with za'atar mixed with olive oil, then baked fast on a very hot surface. It is the course's lesson in a lean yeast dough, where kneading and proofing decide the crumb.
equipment: Large mixing bowl
Baking steel or pizza stone, or a heavy upturned baking tray
Pizza peel or a rimless baking sheet
Baking paper
Kitchen scale
Small bowl and spoon for the za'atar paste
Clean tea towel

ingredients.item: Extra virgin olive oil for the topping
To serve: tomato, cucumber, fresh mint, olives, labneh

mise: Warm the water to about 100°F (38°C): it should feel just warm on the inside of your wrist.
Place the steel or stone on the top rack and heat the oven to its maximum, 500 to 550°F (260 to 290°C), for at least 45 minutes before baking.
Mix the za'atar and olive oil into a loose paste; it should look generously oily.
Cut 6 squares of baking paper slightly larger than each flatbread.
Slice tomato and cucumber and pick mint leaves for serving.

timeline.do: Mix and knead the dough, 8 to 10 minutes.
First rise, about 1 hour. Mix the za'atar paste.
Oven and steel on to heat at maximum.
Divide into 6 balls; rest 15 minutes.
Shape, top and bake one or two at a time, 4 to 6 minutes each.
Fold around tomato, cucumber and mint and serve warm.

steps.do: Mix the flour, yeast, sugar and salt in the bowl. Add the warm water and olive oil and stir to a shaggy dough. Tip onto the counter and knead for 8 to 10 minutes, pushing the dough away with the heel of your hand, folding it back and turning it.
steps.look: The dough changes from rough and sticky to smooth, soft and elastic.
steps.mistake: Adding lots of flour because the dough is sticky at first, which makes it dry and tough.
steps.fix: Keep kneading; stickiness lessens as gluten develops. Oil your hands instead of flouring the counter.

steps.do: Test with the windowpane test: pinch off a small piece and stretch it slowly between your fingers.
steps.look: It stretches thin enough to let light through without tearing, like a windowpane.
steps.mistake: Stopping before the gluten is developed, which gives a dense, tearing flatbread.
steps.fix: If it tears quickly, knead 2 more minutes and test again.

steps.do: Shape into a ball, place in a lightly oiled bowl, cover with a towel and leave in a warm place for about 1 hour.
steps.look: The dough doubles in size, feels airy, and a floured finger pressed in leaves a dent that springs back slowly.
steps.mistake: A cold kitchen, so the dough barely rises.
steps.fix: Put it in an oven with only the light on, or near a warm spot; give it longer.

steps.do: Press out the air, divide into 6 equal pieces, about 4 oz (110 g) each, and roll each into a tight ball. Cover and rest for 15 minutes.
steps.look: Smooth, tight balls that relax slightly while resting.
steps.mistake: Skipping the rest, so the dough springs back when shaping.
steps.fix: Give it the rest; it relaxes the gluten.

steps.do: On a piece of baking paper, press and stretch one ball with your fingertips into a round about 8 inches (20 cm) across and 1/8 inch (3 mm) thick, leaving a slightly thicker rim. Dimple the centre all over with your fingertips.
steps.look: A thin, even round with a small rim and little dimples in the surface.
steps.mistake: Rolling with a pin and pressing out all the air, which makes a crisp cracker rather than soft bread.
steps.fix: Use fingertips; it keeps some bubbles in the dough.

steps.do: Spoon about 2 tbsp (30 ml) za'atar paste over the centre and spread it right up to the rim.
steps.look: A dark green, glistening layer filling the dimples, generous enough to look excessive.
steps.mistake: A thin, timid layer that bakes dry and pale.
steps.fix: Be generous; the oil keeps the za'atar from burning and gives the right flavour.

steps.do: Slide the paper and bread onto the peel, then onto the hot steel. Bake for 4 to 6 minutes.
steps.look: The rim puffs and turns golden with blistered spots, the base is crisp and spotted, the za'atar bubbles and smells of toasted thyme and sesame.
steps.mistake: A not-hot-enough oven, so the bread dries out before it browns.
steps.fix: Heat the steel for the full 45 minutes. If your oven runs cool, finish under the overhead grill (broiler) for 30 seconds, watching closely.

steps.do: Serve hot: fold or roll each man'oushe around tomato, cucumber and mint, or eat flat with labneh and olives.
steps.look: A soft, chewy flatbread with a crisp edge that folds without cracking.
steps.mistake: Leaving it to cool for too long, so it toughens.
steps.fix: Stack finished breads under a towel and eat within 15 minutes.

science: Kneading builds gluten: two flour proteins, glutenin and gliadin, hydrate and link into long, stretchy chains that trap gas. The windowpane test shows those chains are strong and aligned enough to stretch thin without breaking. During proofing, yeast eats sugars and releases carbon dioxide and alcohol, inflating the gluten network and adding flavour. A very hot steel delivers heat quickly, so water in the dough turns to steam and puffs the rim before the crust sets. The thin bread bakes in minutes, so it stays soft inside. Za'atar is mixed with oil because the herbs and sesame would scorch dry in such heat, while oil protects them, conducts heat and carries the fat-soluble aromas.
plating: Serve flat on a wooden board, cut into quarters if sharing, with a small bowl of labneh, olives, and a plate of sliced tomato, cucumber and mint leaves alongside. Or roll each one into a cone around the vegetables and wrap the bottom in paper as Lebanese bakeries do.

pairing.drink: Mint tea or a cold glass of ayran in the morning; at lunch, a dry rosé with the herbs and tomato.
pairing.brennans: Minuty ‘Prestige’ Côtes de Provence Rosé 2024: a dry, herby Provençal rosé that suits thyme, sumac and olive oil.

variations: Man'oushe jibneh: cheese instead of za'atar, using grated akkawi or mozzarella.
Half and half: za'atar on one half, cheese on the other.
Lahm bi ajeen: a topping of spiced minced lamb, tomato and onion.
safety: A baking steel at 500 to 550°F (260 to 290°C) causes serious burns; use oven gloves and a peel, and never reach in by hand.
Let the steel cool in the oven for several hours before moving it.

title: Blini with Smetana
summary: Small, airy pancakes made from a yeasted buckwheat and wheat batter lightened with whipped egg whites, brushed with butter and served with smetana. They put two kinds of rise in one bite, yeast and whipped whites, and train the hand to make small, even pancakes.
equipment: Large mixing bowl
Clean, grease-free bowl and a whisk or electric hand mixer for the whites
Large spatula for folding
Heavy nonstick or cast iron frying pan, or a flat griddle
Tablespoon or small ladle
Pastry brush
Warm plate and a tea towel

ingredients.note: plus more for the pan and brushing

ingredients.item: To serve: smoked salmon, salmon roe, jam or honey

mise: Warm the milk to about 100°F (38°C).
Separate the eggs carefully: not a speck of yolk in the whites, or they will not whip.
Melt the butter; keep extra melted butter in a small dish with a brush for the finished blini.
Set a warm plate and a folded tea towel beside the stove.

timeline.do: Make the yeasted batter; rise 1 hour until bubbly.
Whisk the whites and fold them into the batter.
Rest 10 minutes, then cook in batches, about 2 minutes per batch.
Serve the stack warm with smetana and toppings.

steps.do: Whisk both flours, yeast, sugar and salt in the large bowl. Whisk the egg yolks and melted butter into the warm milk, then pour into the flour and whisk to a smooth batter.
steps.look: A smooth, thick batter, like heavy cream, light grey-brown from the buckwheat.
steps.mistake: Hot milk, which kills the yeast so the batter never bubbles.
steps.fix: If no bubbles appear after 30 minutes, the yeast is dead; whisk in another 1 tsp (3 g) yeast dissolved in a little warm milk.

steps.do: Cover and leave in a warm place for 1 hour.
steps.look: The batter rises by about half and the surface is covered in bubbles; it smells pleasantly yeasty and slightly sour.
steps.mistake: Rushing the rise, which gives flat, bland blini.
steps.fix: Give it time in a warm spot; buckwheat batters are slower than wheat.

steps.do: Whisk the egg whites in the clean bowl until they hold soft peaks that droop slightly at the tip.
steps.look: White, glossy foam; lifted on the whisk, the peak curls over.
steps.mistake: Whipping too stiff, so the whites become dry and grainy and will not fold in smoothly.
steps.fix: Stop at soft peaks. If overwhipped, whisk in 1 tbsp (15 ml) of unwhipped white to loosen them.

steps.do: Stir a third of the whites into the batter to loosen it, then gently fold in the rest with the spatula: cut down through the middle, sweep along the bottom and lift over, turning the bowl.
steps.look: A light, airy batter with no streaks of white.
steps.mistake: Stirring hard, which knocks out the air.
steps.fix: Fold slowly and stop as soon as the white disappears.

steps.do: Rest the batter for 10 minutes. Heat the pan over medium heat and brush with butter. Drop tablespoons of batter, spacing them 1 inch (2.5 cm) apart, to make blini about 2 1/2 inches (6 cm) across.
steps.look: The batter sizzles gently and spreads a little into neat rounds.
steps.mistake: Too hot a pan, so the outside burns while the inside is raw.
steps.fix: Lower the heat; the first batch is a test.

steps.do: Cook for 1 minute, until bubbles rise and pop on the surface and the edges look dry, then flip and cook 30 to 60 seconds more.
steps.look: Golden, lacy edges and a soft, puffy, open crumb.
steps.mistake: Flipping before the bubbles appear, so the blini break apart.
steps.fix: Wait for the bubbles and the dry edge.

steps.do: Move to the warm plate, brush each with melted butter and stack them, covered with the tea towel. Butter the pan between batches.
steps.look: A glistening stack of soft, golden blini.
steps.mistake: Leaving them uncovered, so they dry out.
steps.fix: Keep the stack covered; the steam keeps them soft.

steps.do: Serve warm with smetana and your toppings.
steps.look: Soft, tangy, yeasty blini with a cool spoon of smetana.
steps.mistake: Serving them cold from the stack.
steps.fix: Warm in a low oven, covered, for 5 minutes if needed.

science: Two leaveners work together. Yeast ferments sugars in the batter, producing carbon dioxide and flavourful acids and alcohols that give blini their slightly sour, complex taste. Buckwheat has no gluten, so wheat flour provides enough gluten to trap some of that gas. Whipped egg whites add a second, mechanical rise: whisking unfolds the egg proteins, which then form a network around tiny air bubbles. Folding keeps those bubbles intact. In the pan, heat expands both the carbon dioxide and the trapped air, while the proteins set around them, so the blini puff with an open, tender crumb. Bubbles rising and popping on top show that the structure below has set enough to flip.
plating: Stack the blini in a slightly overlapping fan on a warm plate. Top three or four individually with a teaspoon of smetana and a small curl of smoked salmon or a few beads of salmon roe, and serve the rest plain alongside bowls of smetana and jam.

pairing.drink: A glass of brut Champagne or chilled vodka; both cut the butter and suit salmon or roe.
pairing.brennans: Charles Lafitte Brut Champagne NV: a crisp brut that does exactly what Champagne has always done for blini, roe and smetana.

variations: All-wheat blini: replace the buckwheat with plain flour for a milder flavour.
Large Russian blini: use a full ladle of a thinner batter in a large pan, for blini wrapped around fillings.
Sweet blini: serve with honey, jam and a dusting of sugar.
safety: Keep salmon roe and smoked salmon refrigerated until serving.
Batter containing raw egg yolk should be used within 2 to 3 hours of making.

title: Sticky Buns
summary: Soft, enriched yeast buns rolled with butter, brown sugar and cinnamon, baked on top of a caramel and pecan base, then flipped so the glossy topping runs over the spirals. An enriched dough proves slowly and teaches patience, and the dish ends on a caramel lesson.
equipment: Stand mixer with dough hook, or a large bowl
9 by 13 inch (23 by 33 cm) metal baking tin
Saucepan for the caramel
Rolling pin
Unflavoured dental floss or a sharp serrated knife
Large tray or board bigger than the tin, for inverting
Oven gloves
Instant-read thermometer

ingredients.item: Unsalted butter, softened, for the dough
Dark brown sugar for the caramel
Unsalted butter, softened, for the filling
Light brown sugar for the filling

mise: Warm the milk to about 100°F (38°C).
Soften all the butter for the dough and filling.
Toast the pecans in a dry pan over medium heat for 4 to 5 minutes, shaking, until fragrant.
Mix the filling sugar and cinnamon in a bowl.
Find a tray or board bigger than the tin for flipping.

timeline.do: Make and knead the dough, 10 minutes; first rise 90 minutes.
Make the caramel and pour into the tin with pecans.
Roll, fill, roll up and cut 12 buns; set on the caramel. Second rise 45 to 60 minutes.
Heat the oven to 350°F (175°C).
Bake 30 to 35 minutes.
Rest exactly 5 minutes; invert. Cool 10 minutes before serving.

steps.do: Mix the flour, yeast, sugar and salt. Add the warm milk and eggs and mix to a dough. Knead for 5 minutes, then add the softened butter a tablespoon at a time, kneading until each piece disappears. Knead 5 minutes more.
steps.look: A very soft, smooth, glossy dough that pulls away from the sides of the bowl and passes the windowpane test.
steps.mistake: Adding the butter at the start, which coats the flour and stops gluten forming.
steps.fix: Build gluten first, then knead in butter gradually; the dough will look greasy for a minute, then come together.

steps.do: Cover and leave to rise in a warm place for about 90 minutes.
steps.look: Doubled in size, soft and pillowy.
steps.mistake: Expecting it to rise as fast as a lean dough.
steps.fix: Butter, sugar and egg slow the yeast; give it the full time in a warm spot.

steps.do: Make the caramel: melt the 170 g butter, dark brown sugar, honey and salt in the saucepan over medium heat, stirring until the sugar dissolves and it bubbles for 1 minute. Pour into the tin, spread evenly and scatter the pecans over, flat side up.
steps.look: A smooth, glossy, bubbling caramel, the colour of milk chocolate.
steps.mistake: Boiling the caramel hard, which makes it set too firm and chewy.
steps.fix: One minute of bubbling is enough; it cooks further in the oven.

steps.do: Roll the dough on a lightly floured surface into a rectangle about 12 by 18 inches (30 by 45 cm). Spread the softened filling butter evenly to the edges, leaving a 1 inch (2.5 cm) strip bare along one long side. Sprinkle the cinnamon sugar evenly and press it in lightly.
steps.look: An even rectangle covered in a thick layer of cinnamon sugar.
steps.mistake: Melted butter instead of softened, which runs out and makes the filling leak.
steps.fix: Use soft, spreadable butter.

steps.do: Roll up tightly from the long (18 inch (45 cm)) side towards the bare strip, pinching the seam closed. Cut into 12 equal pieces with floss or a serrated knife.
steps.look: A tight spiral in each cut face, about 1 1/2 inches (4 cm) thick.
steps.mistake: Pressing down with a blunt knife, which squashes the spirals.
steps.fix: Slide floss under the log, cross the ends over the top and pull to cut cleanly.

steps.do: Arrange the buns cut side down on the caramel in rows of three by four. Cover and rise for 45 to 60 minutes. Heat the oven to 350°F (175°C).
steps.look: The buns puff and touch each other.
steps.mistake: Overproofing, so the buns collapse in the oven.
steps.fix: Check at 45 minutes: a gently pressed bun should spring back slowly.

steps.do: Bake for 30 to 35 minutes.
steps.look: Deep golden brown tops, caramel bubbling up at the edges, and the centre of a middle bun reads 190°F (88°C).
steps.mistake: Underbaking, so the centre buns are doughy.
steps.fix: If the tops brown too fast, cover loosely with foil and bake until the centre reaches temperature.

steps.do: Rest exactly 5 minutes, then put the tray upside down over the tin and, wearing oven gloves, flip in one firm movement. Lift the tin away slowly and scrape any caramel or pecans left in the tin onto the buns.
steps.look: Glossy caramel dripping down the spirals, pecans on top.
steps.mistake: Waiting too long, so the caramel sets in the tin, or flipping straight away, so it runs everywhere.
steps.fix: If caramel has set, put the tin back in the oven for 2 minutes to loosen it, then flip.

steps.do: Cool for 10 minutes before pulling apart and serving.
steps.look: The caramel thickens and clings as it cools.
steps.mistake: Biting straight away; the caramel is scalding hot.
steps.fix: Let them cool; they are better warm than hot.

science: An enriched dough contains butter, eggs and sugar. Fat coats the gluten proteins and shortens the strands, making the crumb tender rather than chewy, while sugar competes with yeast for water and slows fermentation, so rising takes longer. That is why the butter goes in after the gluten has formed. In the caramel, honey or golden syrup contains glucose and fructose, which interfere with sucrose crystals forming, keeping the topping smooth rather than grainy. Baking caramelises the sugars further. The five minute rest matters: right out of the oven the caramel is runny, but as it cools a little it thickens enough to cling when the tin is turned out, yet stays liquid enough to release.
plating: Serve the buns on the tray they were inverted onto, as a pull-apart slab, or lift individual buns onto plates, pecan side up, and spoon any caramel from the tray over the top. A cup of strong coffee alongside.

pairing.drink: A New Orleans coffee with chicory, or a glass of tawny Port with a late brunch.
pairing.brennans: Café Brûlot Coffee Cake: Brennan's own sweet breakfast course, a chicory coffee and chocolate cake with pecans and a spiced citrus glaze; set beside these buns it shows guests another way a sweet bake carries pecans and spice.

variations: Cinnamon rolls: bake without the caramel base and finish with a cream cheese icing.
Orange and cardamom: add orange zest to the dough and ground cardamom to the filling.
Overnight: after cutting and arranging the buns, cover and refrigerate overnight, then let them rise for 1 hour before baking.
safety: Hot caramel causes severe burns; wear oven gloves, flip over a tray away from you, and keep children clear.
Never taste caramel straight from the pan.

title: Avgolemono Soup
summary: A Greek chicken soup made from a clear stock with orzo and shredded chicken, thickened at the end with eggs and lemon juice tempered with hot broth until it turns velvety. Stock begins here, and the egg and lemon liaison teaches tempering, the skill that keeps eggs from curdling in every custard and sauce to come.
skills: tempering egg and lemon with hot broth
equipment: Large stockpot, at least 6 quarts (6 litres)
Ladle and a fine skimmer or large spoon
Fine sieve, lined with muslin if you have it
Large heatproof bowl and a balloon whisk
Medium saucepan for the finished soup
Instant-read thermometer
Two forks for shredding

ingredients.item: Bone-in chicken thighs and drumsticks, or a small whole chicken cut up

ingredients.note: from about 2 lemons, plus wedges to serve

mise: Take the eggs out of the fridge 30 minutes ahead; cold eggs scramble more easily.
Cut the vegetables in large pieces for the stock.
Squeeze the lemons and strain out the pips.
Chop the dill.
Set the sieve over a large bowl or pot ready for straining.

timeline.do: Chicken into cold water, bring slowly to a simmer and skim.
Add vegetables and aromatics; simmer gently 1 1/2 hours.
Lift out the chicken, strain the stock, skim the fat; shred the meat.
Cook the orzo in 6 cups (1.4 litres) of the stock, 8 to 10 minutes.
Whisk eggs and lemon; temper with hot stock; return off the heat.
Warm gently to thicken, add chicken and dill, serve.

steps.do: Put the chicken in the stockpot and cover with the cold water. Bring slowly to a simmer over medium heat, about 20 minutes. As it heats, grey foam will rise; skim it off with the skimmer.
steps.look: Grey foam gathering on the surface just before the simmer; after skimming, the liquid is clear and pale.
steps.mistake: Bringing it to a rolling boil, which churns the foam and fat back in and makes a cloudy stock.
steps.fix: Lower the heat the moment you see the first bubbles. Skim regularly for the first 15 minutes.

steps.do: Add the onion, carrot, celery, bay and peppercorns. Hold the stock at a bare simmer, with bubbles just breaking the surface, uncovered, for 1 1/2 hours.
steps.look: A gentle shiver on the surface with an occasional bubble. The stock turns golden and smells deeply of chicken.
steps.mistake: Covering and boiling, which emulsifies fat into the liquid and clouds it.
steps.fix: Keep the lid off and the heat low; top up with a little water if it drops below the chicken.

steps.do: Lift the chicken onto a plate. Pour the stock through the sieve, discard the vegetables, and spoon off as much of the fat floating on top as you can. Season the stock with the salt. When cool enough, shred the meat with two forks, discarding skin and bones.
steps.look: A clear, golden stock with only a few beads of fat; about 7 to 8 cups (1.7 to 1.9 litres).
steps.mistake: Pressing the vegetables through the sieve, which clouds the stock.
steps.fix: Let it drip through; patience gives clarity.

steps.do: Bring 6 cups (1.4 litres) of the stock to a simmer in the saucepan, add the orzo and cook for 8 to 10 minutes, stirring now and then, until tender.
steps.look: Plump, soft orzo; the stock slightly clouded by its starch.
steps.mistake: Overcooking the orzo, which goes mushy and soaks up the soup.
steps.fix: Taste from 7 minutes; it continues to soften in the hot soup.

steps.do: Whisk the eggs in the large heatproof bowl for 1 minute until frothy and pale, then whisk in the lemon juice.
steps.look: A light, foamy yellow mixture.
steps.mistake: Under-whisking, so egg white strands cook into threads.
steps.fix: Whisk until completely uniform with no clear white visible.

steps.do: Temper the eggs: whisking constantly, add one ladle of hot stock in a thin stream. Then add a second ladle, and a third, still whisking.
steps.look: The egg mixture warms and thickens slightly, staying smooth and creamy with no flecks.
steps.mistake: Pouring the hot stock in too fast, which scrambles the eggs instantly.
steps.fix: If a few flecks appear, keep going and strain the mixture before returning it. If it has fully curdled, start again with fresh eggs.

steps.do: Take the soup pan off the heat. Pour the tempered egg mixture slowly into the pan, stirring all the time.
steps.look: The soup turns pale, opaque and creamy.
steps.mistake: Pouring the egg into soup that is still boiling, which curdles it.
steps.fix: Always off the heat. If the soup has just been boiling, wait 1 minute first.

steps.do: Return to low heat and stir gently for 2 to 4 minutes until the soup thickens and reaches 160 to 170°F (71 to 77°C). Do not let it simmer. Stir in the chicken and dill, taste and season with salt and pepper.
steps.look: A velvety soup that coats the back of a spoon, pale as ivory, with steam rising but no bubbles.
steps.mistake: Letting it boil, which turns it into lemony egg drop soup.
steps.fix: Keep it below the simmer; use the thermometer. If it begins to curdle, take it off the heat and whisk hard.

science: A good stock extracts gelatin from bones and skin and flavour from meat and vegetables. Starting in cold water and heating slowly lets proteins dissolve and then clump into foam that can be skimmed; a gentle simmer keeps fat from emulsifying into the liquid, so the stock stays clear. Avgolemono is thickened by egg proteins. Egg yolk proteins thicken from about 150°F (65°C) and set solid not far above that, so if hot stock hits egg directly, the proteins bond too tightly and curdle. Tempering warms the eggs gradually while diluting them, so they thicken smoothly. Lemon juice helps, because acid slows the bonding of egg proteins. The orzo's starch also guards against curdling.
plating: Ladle into warm wide bowls, making sure each has an even share of chicken and orzo. Finish with a pinch of chopped dill, a twist of black pepper and a thin lemon slice floating in the centre. Serve with lemon wedges and crusty bread.

pairing.drink: A crisp, lemony Greek white such as Assyrtiko, whose acidity matches the lemon in the soup.
pairing.brennans: Gaia ‘Wild Ferment’ Assyrtiko Santorini 2023: a Santorini Assyrtiko, the natural Greek match for egg and lemon.

variations: Avgolemono with rice: use short grain rice instead of orzo, cooked 15 to 18 minutes.
Kotosoupa: serve the chicken pieces whole, on the side, with the soup.
Avgolemono sauce: use the same liaison with less stock to make a sauce for stuffed vine leaves or meatballs.
safety: Chicken must reach 165°F (74°C); after 1 1/2 hours of simmering it is well beyond this.
Cool leftover stock quickly in a shallow container and refrigerate within 2 hours; use within 4 days.
Reheat the finished soup gently, not to the boil, but until steaming, 165°F (74°C).

Roll and cut the noodles.
Strain the stock and skim the fat.

steps.mistake: Boiling hard, so the foam breaks up and clouds the stock.

steps.mistake: Not enough flour, so the noodles stick together in a clump.

steps.mistake: Pressing the solids, which clouds the stock.

steps.do: Bring the stock to a simmer, add the diced onion, carrot and celery and cook for 8 to 10 minutes until just tender. Add the noodles and simmer 3 to 4 minutes. Shred the chicken into bite-size pieces and add it to heat through for 1 minute.
steps.look: Noodles plump and tender, vegetables bright and soft, chicken hot.

title: Hainanese Chicken Rice

rice cooked in stock and chicken fat

ingredients.item: Fine salt for the poaching water

ingredients.note: rinsed until clear and drained 30 minutes

ingredients.item: Chicken fat (from the cavity) or neutral oil
Lime juice and sugar for sauce

ingredients.item: Light soy sauce and sesame oil

Mince the garlic and ginger for the rice; prepare the sauce ingredients.

Bring water to the boil; lower in the chicken and poach below a simmer, 40 to 50 minutes.

Fry garlic and ginger in chicken fat; add rice; cook in broth 15 minutes plus 10 resting.
Blend the chilli sauce. Slice cucumber. Heat broth for soup.
Chop the chicken; dress with soy and sesame.

steps.do: Bring the water, ginger, spring onions and 1 tbsp (18 g) salt to the boil in the stockpot. Holding the chicken by the legs (or with a large hook or spoon in the cavity), lower it in, lift it out to drain the cavity, and lower it in again three times. Then submerge it, breast side down.
steps.look: The skin tightens slightly each time; the water in the cavity is the same temperature as the pot.
steps.mistake: Dropping the cold chicken straight in, so the cavity stays cold and the thighs undercook.
steps.fix: The dip and drain evens out the temperature inside and out.

steps.do: Bring back to just under a simmer, then turn the heat to low and hold the water at 175 to 185°F (80 to 85°C), with a few small bubbles at the edge. Poach for 40 to 50 minutes depending on size.
steps.look: The water shivers but never bubbles across the surface. The skin turns pale and smooth.
steps.mistake: Letting it boil, which tears the skin and makes the meat stringy and dry.
steps.fix: Keep the thermometer in the water and adjust the heat. If it boils, add a cup of cold water.

steps.do: Check doneness by inserting the thermometer into the thickest part of the thigh, not touching bone.
steps.look: The thigh reads 165°F (74°C) and the juices run clear when pierced.
steps.mistake: Guessing by time, so the bird is undercooked at the joint.
steps.fix: If below temperature, return it to the pot for 5 to 10 minutes more.

steps.do: Lift the chicken out, letting the liquid drain from the cavity back into the pot, and plunge it into the iced water for 10 minutes. Then hang or set it on a rack to drain.
steps.look: The skin tightens and turns smooth, firm and slightly translucent, with a jelly-like layer beneath.
steps.mistake: Skipping the ice bath, so the skin is loose and flabby.
steps.fix: Use plenty of ice; top it up if it melts.

steps.mistake: Browning the garlic, which turns bitter.
steps.fix: Keep the heat medium and stir constantly.

steps.do: Bring to the boil, cover tightly, turn the heat to its lowest and cook 15 minutes. Turn off and rest covered for 10 minutes.
steps.look: Glossy, separate grains, fragrant with ginger and chicken fat.
steps.mistake: Lifting the lid during cooking.
steps.fix: Trust the time; if still firm, sprinkle with 2 tbsp (30 ml) hot broth and rest 5 more minutes.

steps.do: Blend the chillies, garlic, ginger, lime juice, sugar, a pinch of salt and 3 tbsp (45 ml) hot broth to a coarse sauce. Taste: it should be hot, sharp and gingery.

steps.mistake: Too little acid, so the sauce tastes flat.
steps.fix: Add more lime juice and a pinch of salt until it is lively.

science: Poaching well below boiling heats the chicken slowly and evenly, so the outside does not overcook and squeeze out moisture before the thighs reach a safe 165°F (74°C). Ginger scallion oil: pour hot oil over minced ginger, spring onion and salt for a second sauce.

title: Soupe à l'Oignon Gratinée
summary: French onion soup: a kilo of onions coloured slowly over an hour to deep mahogany, simmered in beef stock with wine and thyme, and finished under the overhead grill (broiler) with toasted bread and melted Gruyère. It teaches patience at the stove, a brown stock and gratinating.

ingredients.note: about 5 large, halved and sliced 1/8 inch (3 mm) thick
home-made or good quality low salt

Heat the stock in a separate pan.
Grate the cheese.
Toast the baguette slices in a 400°F (200°C) oven for 8 to 10 minutes until dry and golden.
Set the ovenproof bowls on the baking tray.

Cook the onions, stirring and scraping, 45 to 60 minutes to mahogany.
Flour in; deglaze with wine; add stock and herbs; simmer 20 minutes. Toast the bread.
Heat the grill; season the soup.
Ladle into bowls, top with bread and cheese, grill 3 to 5 minutes.

steps.do: Melt the butter in the Dutch oven over medium heat. Add all the onions and the salt, stir to coat, cover and cook for 10 minutes, stirring once or twice.
steps.look: The onions collapse, release liquid and turn soft and translucent.
steps.mistake: Starting on high heat, so the edges burn before the onions soften.
steps.fix: Begin covered on medium so they sweat first; the salt draws out water.

steps.do: Uncover, lower to medium-low and cook for 35 to 50 minutes more, stirring every 3 to 5 minutes and scraping the brown film from the bottom of the pot back into the onions.
steps.look: The onions go from pale gold to amber to deep, glossy mahogany brown, and shrink to about a fifth of their volume. They smell sweet and jammy. A brown crust forms on the pan bottom between stirs.
steps.mistake: Raising the heat to hurry, which gives bitter, burnt edges on raw centres.
steps.fix: If the bottom browns too fast or begins to look black, add 2 tbsp (30 ml) water and scrape; the browned bits dissolve into the onions.

steps.do: Sprinkle in the flour and stir for 1 minute. Pour in the wine and scrape the bottom of the pot hard to dissolve every bit of fond. Simmer for 2 minutes until the wine has mostly evaporated.
steps.look: A rush of steam, the pan bottom comes clean, and the onions become glossy and thick.
steps.mistake: Leaving brown bits stuck to the pan, losing flavour.
steps.fix: Scrape with the flat edge of the spatula until the bottom is clean.

steps.do: Add the hot stock, thyme and bay. Bring to a simmer and cook gently, uncovered, for 20 minutes. Stir in the Cognac if using, remove the herbs, taste and season with salt and pepper.
steps.look: A deep brown, glossy soup with soft onions suspended in it.
steps.mistake: Seasoning too early, before the stock reduces.
steps.fix: Season at the end; if too salty, add a splash of water.

steps.do: Heat the overhead grill to high with a rack 6 inches (15 cm) below. Ladle the hot soup into the bowls on the tray, filling to about 1/2 inch (1 cm) from the rim.
steps.look: Bowls full of steaming soup.
steps.mistake: Filling to the brim, so the cheese and soup spill over and burn on the tray.
steps.fix: Leave a little room at the top.

steps.do: Float two slices of toasted baguette on each bowl so they cover the surface, then pile the cheese on top, letting it reach the rims.
steps.look: A thick, even blanket of cheese over the bread, touching the edges.
steps.mistake: Using untoasted bread, which sinks and turns to mush.
steps.fix: Toast the bread until dry and crisp first.

steps.do: Grill for 3 to 5 minutes, watching constantly.
steps.look: The cheese melts, bubbles and browns in deep golden and dark spots, sealing the bowl.
steps.mistake: Walking away, so the cheese burns black.
steps.fix: Stand at the oven and turn the tray if one side browns faster.

steps.do: Using oven gloves, set each bowl on a plate lined with a folded napkin and serve immediately.
steps.look: Bubbling, browned cheese with soup steaming at the edges.
steps.mistake: Placing the hot bowl straight on the table or a cold surface, which can crack it.
steps.fix: Always on a plate with a napkin underneath.

Under the grill, intense radiant heat browns the cheese fast through the Maillard reaction while melting it into a crust.
plating: Serve each bowl on a plate lined with a folded napkin, which stops it sliding and protects the table. The cheese should drape over the rim slightly. Give each guest a spoon and a knife for the cheese.

title: Barszcz Czerwony with Uszka
summary: A jewel-clear, sour beetroot broth served with uszka, tiny dumplings filled with wild mushrooms and onion. It pairs the skill of a clear, carefully soured broth with the first hand-folded dumplings in the course.

Chop the filling mushrooms and onion finely.

steps.do: Put the beetroot, stock, onion, carrot, parsley root, garlic, bay, allspice and the strained mushroom soaking liquid in the stockpot. Bring to a simmer and cook gently, uncovered, for 40 minutes.

steps.mistake: A wet filling, which makes the dumplings burst.

steps.look: A soft, smooth, elastic dough.
steps.mistake: A stiff dough, which is hard to roll thin and gives tough dumplings.
steps.fix: Knead in a little more water if it resists.

steps.do: Roll the dough very thin, about 1/16 inch (1 to 2 mm), on a floured surface. Cut into 2 inch (5 cm) squares or rounds.
steps.look: Thin, translucent pieces of dough.
steps.mistake: Rolling too thick, so the dumplings are doughy.
steps.fix: Roll thinner; uszka should be delicate.

steps.do: Place a small half teaspoon of filling in the centre of each piece. Fold into a triangle (or half moon) and press the edges together firmly. Then bring the two pointed corners together around your fingertip and pinch them, forming a little ear shape.
steps.look: Tiny dumplings shaped like little ears, sealed all round.
steps.mistake: Too much filling, which stops the edges sealing.
steps.fix: Use less filling; dab the edge with water if it will not stick.

steps.do: Strain the broth through the muslin-lined sieve without pressing. Return it to a clean pan. Add vinegar a tablespoon at a time, then sugar and salt, tasting after each addition.
steps.look: A crystal-clear, garnet broth. It should taste distinctly sour, then slightly sweet, then savoury.
steps.mistake: Boiling the broth after adding the acid, which turns it brown.
steps.fix: Heat it only to just below simmering once soured.

steps.do: Bring a large pan of salted water to the boil. Add the uszka in batches and cook for 2 to 3 minutes after they float to the surface. Lift out with a slotted spoon.
steps.look: The dumplings float and the dough turns tender.
steps.mistake: Overcrowding, so they stick together.
steps.fix: Cook in batches and stir gently once.

plating: Serve in shallow white bowls to show off the colour. Place the uszka in the centre in a small cluster, pour the broth gently around them, and finish with a few sprigs of dill.

title: Gulyásleves (Goulash Soup)

Mortar and pestle or rolling pin for the caraway
Small bowl for the csipetke dough

ingredients.item: Hungarian wax pepper or green bell pepper

Chop the onions finely; mince the garlic; crush the caraway.

Brown the beef in batches.
Sweat the onions 15 minutes until golden; paprika off the heat.

steps.mistake: Browning the onions dark, which makes the soup bitter and muddy coloured.
steps.fix: Keep the heat medium and stir often; add a splash of water if they catch.

steps.do: Take the pot off the heat completely and wait 30 seconds. Stir in the sweet paprika and the hot paprika for 20 seconds until the onions are coated red.
steps.look: The onions turn a vibrant brick red and smell sweet and peppery.
steps.mistake: Adding paprika to a pot on the flame, which scorches it in seconds and makes the whole soup bitter.
steps.fix: If the paprika smells acrid or turns brown, there is no rescue; you must start the onions again.

steps.do: Immediately add the beef and its juices, the garlic, caraway, tomato and pepper and stir. Return to low heat, cover and let the beef stew in its own juices for 30 minutes, stirring now and then and adding a few tablespoons of water if it starts to stick.
steps.look: The beef releases liquid and the base becomes a thick red stew.
steps.mistake: Letting it dry out and burn on the bottom.
steps.fix: Check every 10 minutes and add a splash of water when the juices get low.

steps.do: Pour in the water or stock, add the salt and bring to a simmer. Cover partly and simmer gently for 1 hour.
steps.look: A gentle simmer with a deep red broth and a layer of red fat on top.
steps.mistake: Boiling hard, which toughens the beef.
steps.fix: Lower the heat to a lazy simmer.

steps.do: Add the carrots, parsnips and potatoes. Simmer for 20 to 25 minutes until the vegetables are tender and the beef yields easily to a fork.
steps.look: Soft vegetables, tender beef, and a broth thickened slightly by the potato and onion.
steps.mistake: Adding the vegetables at the start, so they turn to mush.
steps.fix: Vegetables go in for only the last 25 minutes.

steps.do: Flatten the csipetke dough between floured palms to about 1/8 inch (3 mm) and pinch off tiny pieces the size of a fingernail straight into the simmering soup. Cook 3 to 4 minutes.
steps.look: Small, irregular dumplings that rise to the surface and turn firm and tender.
steps.mistake: Pinching pieces too large, so they stay doughy in the centre.
steps.fix: Keep them small; cut one open to check.

steps.do: Taste and season with salt. Serve in warm deep bowls.
steps.look: A glossy, deep red soup with tender beef, vegetables and little dumplings.
steps.mistake: Under-seasoning, so the paprika tastes flat.
steps.fix: Add salt in pinches until the paprika flavour comes alive.

science: Paprika is ground dried peppers, high in sugar and in red carotenoid pigments, which dissolve in fat. Added to fat on a lit burner, the sugars burn within seconds and turn bitter; off the heat, the warm fat gently draws out colour and flavour without scorching. Shin and chuck are rich in collagen. Browning develops flavour through the Maillard reaction, but tenderness comes from long, gentle simmering, during which collagen slowly turns to gelatin, giving the broth body and the beef a soft texture. A hard boil tightens muscle fibres and makes the beef dry. The mass of onions melts into the broth, thickening it without flour. Caraway contributes warm, aniseed-like aromatic oils.
plating: Ladle into warm, deep bowls, giving each a good share of beef, vegetables and csipetke. Add a spoon of soured cream if you like, though it is not traditional, and a pinch of hot paprika. Serve fresh crusty bread on the side.

pairing.drink: A medium-bodied red with soft spice, such as a Hungarian Kékfrankos or a Barbera, whose acidity suits paprika and tomato.
pairing.brennans: La Miraja ‘Le Masche’ Barbera d’Asti 2023: bright acidity and soft tannin to stand up to paprika and beef.

variations: Bean goulash: replace the potatoes with 1 can of drained kidney beans.
Pörkölt: make the stew with very little liquid for the thick paprika stew often called goulash abroad.
Csángó goulash: add sauerkraut for a sour version.
safety: Take the pot off the heat before adding paprika, and keep children back from hot fat.
Cool leftovers quickly and reheat until steaming, 165°F (74°C).

title: Lohikeitto (Finnish Salmon Soup)
summary: A gentle Nordic soup of salmon, potatoes and leek in a quick fish stock made from salmon frames, enriched with cream and finished with plenty of dill. It teaches that fish stock takes twenty minutes and no more, and how to cook salmon gently so it stays moist.
skills: a quick fish stock from salmon frames
equipment: Large saucepan or stockpot for the stock
Medium soup pot
Fine sieve
Skimmer
Fish tweezers or clean pliers for pin bones
Sharp fish knife and board
Ladle

ingredients.item: Salmon frames (bones and head, gills removed)
Dill stalks, bay leaf and allspice berries

ingredients.note: pin bones removed, cut in 1 inch (2.5 cm) cubes
white and pale green, sliced and washed

mise: Rinse the salmon frames under cold water to remove any blood, and make sure the gills are removed; they make stock bitter.
Run your fingers along the fillet to find pin bones and pull them out with tweezers in the direction they lie. Cube the salmon and keep it chilled.
Slice the leek and wash out any grit in a bowl of water.
Peel and dice the potatoes; slice the carrot; chop the dill and keep the stalks for the stock.

timeline.do: Prep the fish and vegetables.
Fish stock: frames in cold water, bring to a simmer, skim, 20 minutes only.
Strain the stock. Sweat leek in butter.
Potatoes and carrot in stock, 12 to 15 minutes.
Cream in; salmon in off the boil, 4 to 5 minutes.
Dill, season, serve.

steps.do: Put the salmon frames in the large saucepan with the cold water, onion, dill stalks, bay and allspice. Bring slowly to a simmer over medium heat and skim off the foam.
steps.look: White foam rising; once skimmed, a clear, pale liquid.
steps.mistake: Boiling hard, which makes the stock cloudy and greasy.
steps.fix: Turn down as soon as it simmers.

steps.do: Simmer very gently for exactly 20 minutes, then strain through the fine sieve without pressing. You should have about 5 cups (1.2 litres).
steps.look: A clear, pale stock that smells fresh and of the sea, not fishy.
steps.mistake: Simmering for an hour as for meat stock, which makes fish stock bitter and gluey.
steps.fix: Set a timer; twenty minutes is all fish bones need.

steps.do: Melt the butter in the soup pot over medium-low heat. Add the leek with a pinch of salt and cook for 5 minutes until soft but not coloured.
steps.look: Soft, glossy, pale green leeks.
steps.mistake: Browning the leeks, which colours and muddies the soup.
steps.fix: Keep the heat low; add a splash of stock if they begin to colour.

steps.do: Add the potatoes, carrot and strained stock. Bring to a simmer and cook for 12 to 15 minutes until the potatoes are just tender.
steps.look: Potato pieces yield to a knife but hold their shape.
steps.mistake: Overcooking the potatoes so they collapse.
steps.fix: Test from 10 minutes.

steps.do: Stir in the cream and bring back to just below a simmer. Season with salt and white pepper.
steps.look: A pale, creamy broth, steaming but not bubbling.
steps.mistake: Boiling the cream hard, which can make it split with the salt in the stock.
steps.fix: Keep it just below the simmer.

steps.do: Add the salmon cubes, turn the heat to low, cover and cook for 4 to 5 minutes without stirring.
steps.look: The salmon turns from deep translucent orange to pale opaque pink and flakes when pressed, but is still moist in the centre.
steps.mistake: Boiling or stirring, so the salmon breaks into shreds and dries out.
steps.fix: Lower the heat and leave it alone; nudge it gently with a spoon only if needed.

steps.do: Stir in most of the dill very gently, taste and adjust the seasoning.
steps.look: A creamy soup flecked with green, chunks of salmon intact.
steps.mistake: Adding the dill too early so it loses its fragrance.
steps.fix: Dill goes in at the end.

steps.do: Ladle into warm bowls and top with the remaining dill.
steps.look: Pink salmon, golden potato and green dill in a pale broth.
steps.mistake: Leaving it on the heat while serving, so the salmon overcooks.
steps.fix: Serve straight away.

science: Fish bones are thin and their collagen is delicate, melting at lower temperatures than land animals'. They release flavour and gelatin in about 20 minutes. Longer cooking extracts bitter compounds from bones and breaks down fats into stale, fishy flavours, which is why fish stock is quick. Salmon muscle is made of short fibres separated by thin layers of connective tissue that melt easily; above about 140°F (60°C) the proteins contract sharply and push out moisture and the white protein called albumin. Cooking the salmon gently in hot, not boiling, liquid keeps it moist. Cream adds fat that carries the flavour of dill, whose aroma compounds are volatile and fade with heat.
plating: Serve in warm, wide bowls so the pieces of salmon sit on top. Arrange a few cubes of salmon visibly on the surface, scatter fresh dill over and add a twist of white pepper. Dark rye bread and butter on the side are traditional.

pairing.drink: A crisp, unoaked Chablis, whose bright acidity and minerality cut the cream and complement the salmon.
pairing.brennans: Louis Michel Chablis 2022: an unoaked Chablis with the acidity and minerality to cut cream and flatter salmon.

variations: Clear lohikeitto: leave out the cream for a lighter soup.
Smoked salmon: replace a third of the salmon with hot-smoked salmon, added at the end.
Allspice and tomato: add a spoon of tomato paste to the leeks for a rosier soup.
safety: Cook salmon until opaque and flaking, 145°F (63°C).
Keep raw fish chilled until the moment it goes into the pot.
Check carefully for pin bones before serving.

title: Seafood Chowder with Brown Soda Bread
summary: An Irish chowder of smoked and fresh fish, mussels and prawns in a light roux-thickened fish stock with bacon, potatoes and cream, served with a quick brown soda bread. It teaches thickening a stock with roux and adding seafood in the order of its cooking time.
skills: adding fish in order of cooking time
equipment: Large heavy soup pot or Dutch oven
Mixing bowl and a wooden spoon for the bread
Baking tray lined with baking paper
Sharp knife and board
Colander for the mussels
Ladle and wooden spoon
Wire rack

ingredients.item: Fish stock (home-made from white fish frames, or good quality)
Firm white fish (cod, hake or haddock)

ingredients.note: plus a little extra if needed

mise: Heat the oven to 425°F (220°C) for the bread.

Scrub the mussels under cold water and pull off the beards. Tap any open ones sharply: discard any that do not close, and any with cracked shells. Keep them in the fridge in a bowl covered with a damp cloth.
Cut all the fish into even chunks and keep chilled, each kind separate.
Dice the bacon, onion, celery and potatoes; slice and wash the leek.
Warm the fish stock.

timeline.do: Oven on. Prep the seafood and vegetables.
Mix and shape the soda bread; bake 40 to 45 minutes.
Render bacon; sweat vegetables; make the roux; add stock and potatoes.
Simmer potatoes until tender, 12 to 15 minutes. Bread out to cool.
Cream in; smoked haddock, then white fish and salmon, then mussels and prawns.
Herbs, pepper, serve with soda bread and butter.

steps.do: For the bread, mix the wholemeal flour, plain flour, bicarbonate and salt in a bowl. Make a well, pour in the buttermilk and mix quickly with a wooden spoon to a soft, sticky dough. Do not knead.
steps.look: A soft, shaggy dough that just holds together.
steps.mistake: Kneading or overmixing, which develops gluten and makes a tough, dense loaf.
steps.fix: Mix just until no dry flour remains; add a splash more buttermilk if very dry.

steps.do: Tip onto the lined tray, shape gently into a round about 2 inches (5 cm) high, sprinkle with oats and cut a deep cross in the top. Bake for 40 to 45 minutes.
steps.look: A dark brown crust; the bottom sounds hollow when tapped.
steps.mistake: Taking it out too soon, leaving a damp middle.
steps.fix: If unsure, bake 5 minutes more upside down on the tray. Cool on a rack under a tea towel for a soft crust.

steps.do: Cook the bacon in the soup pot over medium heat for 5 to 6 minutes until the fat runs and the edges brown. Add the butter, onion, celery and leek and sweat for 6 to 8 minutes until soft but not coloured.
steps.look: Soft, glossy vegetables and crisp-edged bacon.
steps.mistake: Browning the vegetables, which makes the chowder grey.
steps.fix: Lower the heat after the bacon has rendered.

steps.do: Sprinkle in the flour and stir for 2 minutes to cook out the raw taste.
steps.look: The flour coats the vegetables and smells slightly toasty, staying pale.
steps.mistake: Skipping this, so the chowder tastes of raw flour.
steps.fix: Cook the flour fully before the liquid goes in.

steps.do: Gradually add the warm stock, stirring well after each addition. Add the potatoes, bring to a simmer and cook for 12 to 15 minutes until tender.
steps.look: A smooth, lightly thickened broth with tender potatoes.
steps.mistake: Adding the stock all at once, which makes lumps.
steps.fix: Add in three parts, stirring until smooth each time.

steps.do: Stir in the cream and bring back to a gentle simmer. Add the smoked haddock first and cook 2 minutes.
steps.look: The chowder thickens lightly and turns creamy; the haddock begins to turn opaque.
steps.mistake: Adding all the fish at once, so some overcooks and falls apart.
steps.fix: Add seafood in stages by how long it takes to cook.

steps.do: Add the white fish and salmon and cook 2 minutes. Then add the mussels and prawns, cover and cook 2 to 3 minutes more, shaking the pot gently, until the mussels open and the prawns turn pink.
steps.look: Mussel shells open, prawns curled and pink, fish just opaque and holding together.
steps.mistake: Stirring hard, breaking up the fish.
steps.fix: Shake the pot rather than stirring.

steps.do: Discard any mussels that have not opened. Season with black pepper and salt only if needed, and stir in the herbs.
steps.look: A creamy chowder with chunks of fish, open mussels and pink prawns.
steps.mistake: Salting early; the bacon and smoked fish are already salty.
steps.fix: Taste first and season at the end.

steps.do: Ladle into warm bowls and serve with thick slices of soda bread and salted butter.
steps.look: A steaming bowl with seafood on top and bread alongside.
steps.mistake: Letting it simmer on while serving, overcooking the seafood.
steps.fix: Take the pot off the heat as soon as the mussels open.

science: A roux thickens because the flour's starch granules, first coated in fat, absorb liquid and swell when heated, releasing starch that thickens the stock without lumps. Cooking the flour in fat first removes its raw taste. Different seafood cooks at different rates because of size, density and protein type. Smoked haddock is firm and cured; white fish has short, delicate fibres; prawns and mussels cook in minutes and toughen quickly. Adding them in stages means everything finishes at the same time. Soda bread rises without yeast: bicarbonate of soda reacts with the acid in buttermilk to release carbon dioxide immediately, so it is mixed quickly and baked at once before the gas escapes.
plating: Ladle into warm wide bowls, spooning the broth first, then arranging fish chunks, prawns and a few open mussels on top so they show. Finish with chopped chives and a twist of pepper. Serve thick slices of soda bread on a board with a dish of salted butter.

pairing.drink: A Muscadet or a dry Albariño; both are crisp and saline, made for seafood and cream.
pairing.brennans: Domaine de l’Écu ‘Orthogneiss’ Muscadet Sèvre-et-Maine 2022: a mineral, saline Muscadet built for shellfish and creamy broth.

variations: Smoked fish only: use 1 lb (450 g) smoked haddock for a smokier chowder.
Corn chowder: add 1 cup (150 g) sweetcorn kernels with the potatoes.
Without cream: use whole milk for a lighter chowder.
safety: Discard live mussels that are open and do not close when tapped, or that have cracked shells, before cooking; discard any that stay closed after cooking.
Cook fish until opaque and flaking, 145°F (63°C), and prawns until pink and opaque.
Keep seafood chilled until it goes into the pot, and eat the chowder the same day or chill it quickly.

title: Chicken and Andouille Gumbo
summary: The great Cajun gumbo, built on a roux stirred to the colour of dark chocolate, with the trinity of onion, celery and pepper, chicken stock, browned chicken thighs and smoked andouille, served over rice. The dark roux is the most demanding roux in the course and the heart of South Louisiana cooking.
skills: a dark roux stirred to chocolate
equipment: Heavy 6 to 7 quart (6 to 7 litre) cast iron Dutch oven
Flat-edged wooden spatula or roux paddle
Large frying pan for browning
Saucepan for the stock
Ladle and large spoon for skimming
Saucepan for the rice
Long sleeves and a clear, calm hour at the stove
mise: Dice the onion, celery and pepper the same size and put them in one bowl: this is the trinity, and you must have it ready in your hand before the roux is finished. Mince the garlic separately.
Season the chicken with half the Cajun seasoning.
Slice the andouille.
Warm the stock in a saucepan.
Turn off your phone; the roux needs your full attention for up to 45 minutes.

timeline.do: Prep the trinity, chicken, sausage; warm stock.
Brown the sausage and the chicken in a separate pan; set aside.
Stir the roux over medium-low heat, 30 to 45 minutes, to dark chocolate.
Trinity into the roux; garlic; then stock gradually.
Chicken, sausage, bay, thyme in; simmer 1 hour, skimming fat.
Cook the rice.
Season; spring onion and parsley; serve over rice with filé at the table.

steps.do: Brown the andouille in the frying pan over medium heat for 4 to 5 minutes until the edges colour and the fat renders. Lift out. Brown the chicken in the sausage fat in batches, 3 minutes a side. Set aside.
steps.look: Browned sausage edges and golden chicken; a rich fond in the pan.
steps.mistake: Crowding the chicken, so it steams.
steps.fix: Brown in batches. Deglaze the frying pan with a ladle of stock and save it for the gumbo.

steps.do: Heat the oil in the Dutch oven over medium heat for 2 minutes. Whisk in the flour until smooth, then switch to the flat spatula and turn the heat to medium-low. Stir constantly, scraping across the entire bottom and into the corners, in a figure of eight.
steps.look: A smooth paste that bubbles gently.
steps.mistake: A pot that is too thin, which burns the roux in hot spots.
steps.fix: Use heavy cast iron, and keep stirring, especially at the edges.

steps.do: Keep stirring for 30 to 45 minutes as the roux darkens through the stages: blond after 5 minutes, peanut butter after 15, copper penny after 25, and milk chocolate to dark chocolate after 30 to 45. Lower the heat as it darkens.
steps.look: The colour deepens steadily and evenly. It smells nutty, then like toasted bread, then deep and roasted, never burnt. It thins slightly as it darkens.
steps.mistake: Walking away even for a minute, or turning up the heat to hurry. Burnt roux has black specks and smells acrid.
steps.fix: If you see black flecks or smell burning, the roux is ruined: discard it carefully and start again. Do not try to rescue it.

steps.do: When the roux is the colour of dark chocolate, immediately add the trinity all at once and stir hard. Stand back from the steam.
steps.look: A loud sizzle and a burst of steam; the vegetables stop the roux from darkening further, and it smells sweet and toasty.
steps.mistake: Adding the vegetables slowly, so the roux keeps cooking and burns.
steps.fix: Have the trinity in your hand. Tip it in in one go.

steps.do: Cook the trinity in the roux for 5 to 7 minutes, stirring, until softened. Add the garlic for the last minute.
steps.look: The vegetables soften and are coated in the dark roux.
steps.mistake: Burning the garlic.
steps.fix: Garlic goes in last, for just a minute.

steps.do: Gradually add the warm stock a ladle at a time, stirring well after each addition until smooth, then add the rest. Add the browned chicken and sausage, the saved deglazing liquid, the bay, thyme and remaining Cajun seasoning.
steps.look: A smooth, dark brown, glossy liquid, slightly thickened.
steps.mistake: Adding cold stock in one go, which makes the roux lumpy.
steps.fix: Warm stock, added gradually, keeps it smooth.

steps.do: Bring to a simmer, then reduce to low and simmer uncovered for 1 hour, stirring now and then. Skim the oil and foam that rise to the surface with a large spoon.
steps.look: The gumbo deepens in flavour and thickens slightly; a layer of oil gathers on top to be skimmed off.
steps.mistake: Not skimming, so the gumbo is greasy.
steps.fix: Tilt the pot slightly and skim from the edge.

steps.do: Remove the bay and thyme stems. Taste and season with salt, cayenne and hot sauce. Stir in most of the spring onion and parsley.
steps.look: A rich, dark, smoky gumbo with tender chicken.
steps.mistake: Seasoning at the start, before the andouille's salt has come out.
steps.fix: Season at the end.

steps.do: Spoon rice into warm bowls, ladle the gumbo around it and garnish with the remaining spring onion. Offer filé at the table, a pinch per bowl.
steps.look: Dark gumbo around a mound of white rice, flecked with green.
steps.mistake: Boiling filé in the pot, which makes the gumbo stringy.
steps.fix: Filé is added off the heat, at the table.

science: As a roux cooks, its flour proteins and starches brown through the Maillard reaction and starch breakdown, developing deep roasted flavours. The darker it gets, the more the starch breaks into shorter chains, so a dark roux thickens much less than a pale one: gumbo stays relatively thin and brothy, with its body coming partly from gelatin in the stock. A heavy pot holds heat evenly, preventing hot spots that would scorch the flour. The cold, wet vegetables stop the roux cooking instantly by lowering its temperature as their water turns to steam. Filé is ground sassafras leaf; heated in liquid, its carbohydrates thicken and turn stringy, which is why it is sprinkled on at the table.
plating: Pack rice into a small cup and turn it out into the centre of a warm, wide bowl, then ladle the gumbo around the rice so it forms an island. Scatter spring onion and parsley over. Set a small dish of filé and a bottle of hot sauce on the table.

pairing.drink: A cold amber lager, or a Côtes du Rhône with enough spice and fruit for the smoke and heat.
pairing.brennans: Seafood Gumbo: Brennan's own gumbo, worth tasting against this chicken and andouille version to describe roux colour and body to guests.

variations: Okra gumbo: add 8 oz (225 g) sliced okra with the trinity to thicken instead of filé.
Seafood gumbo: leave out the chicken, use seafood stock and add shrimp, crab and oysters in the last 5 minutes.
Gumbo z'herbes: a greens gumbo with many kinds of greens.
safety: Hot roux can reach well over 400°F (200°C) and sticks to skin; stir with a long-handled spatula, wear long sleeves, keep children away and never taste it hot.
Chicken must reach 165°F (74°C); after an hour of simmering it is well beyond this.
Cool leftovers quickly; gumbo is often better the next day, reheated until steaming.

title: Roast Beef Po' Boy with Debris Gravy
summary: The New Orleans sandwich of beef pot-roasted slowly in the oven, sliced and soaked in a gravy made from its drippings and the shreds that fall off the roast, the debris, piled into crisp French bread and dressed with lettuce, tomato, pickles and mayonnaise. It teaches the covered oven braise, resting and making gravy from what the roast leaves behind.
skills: making gravy from the drippings and debris
equipment: Heavy Dutch oven or roasting tin with a tight lid or foil
Instant-read thermometer
Saucepan for the gravy and a whisk
Sharp carving knife and board with a juice groove
Fat separator or a heatproof jug and spoon
Bread knife
Tongs

ingredients.note: in one piece, tied if loose

ingredients.item: New Orleans style French bread (light, crisp crust)

mise: Take the beef out of the fridge 1 hour before cooking and pat it dry. Season it all over with salt, pepper and garlic powder.
Heat the oven to 300°F (150°C).
Slice the onion and smash the garlic.
Shred the lettuce, slice the tomatoes and drain the pickles; keep them chilled.
Make sure the bread is fresh; po' boy bread is best the day it is baked.

timeline.do: Season the beef; oven to 300°F (150°C).
Sear the beef on all sides, about 12 minutes.
Onions, garlic, stock in; covered into the oven 3 1/2 hours.
Rest the beef 20 minutes; skim the drippings; make the roux and gravy.
Slice or pull the beef; return it with the debris to the gravy.
Warm the bread briefly; dress and build.
Cut and serve with lots of napkins.

steps.do: Heat the oil in the Dutch oven over medium-high heat until it shimmers. Sear the beef for 3 minutes on each side, including the ends, until a deep brown crust forms all over. Lift out onto a plate.
steps.look: A dark, even crust and a brown fond on the base of the pot. The beef releases from the pot when it is ready to turn.
steps.mistake: Moving the beef too soon, so it sticks and tears instead of browning.
steps.fix: Leave it until it releases on its own.

steps.do: Lower the heat to medium, add the onion and garlic and cook 5 minutes, scraping the fond. Pour in the stock and Worcestershire, scraping again, and add the bay and thyme. Return the beef.
steps.look: The liquid comes about a third of the way up the beef and turns rich brown as the fond dissolves.
steps.mistake: Covering the beef entirely with liquid, which boils rather than roasts the top.
steps.fix: Liquid should come only partway up.

steps.do: Cover tightly and roast in the oven at 300°F (150°C) for 3 1/2 hours, turning the beef once halfway.
steps.look: The beef shrinks and darkens; a fork slides in with no resistance and the meat begins to fall apart at the edges.
steps.mistake: Checking for tenderness too early and taking it out tough.
steps.fix: Chuck needs time to tenderise; if a fork meets resistance, give it 30 more minutes. It will be around 200°F (93°C) inside when ready.

steps.do: Lift the beef onto the board and rest it, loosely covered with foil, for 20 minutes. Strain the cooking liquid into a fat separator or jug, keeping the softened onion and any shreds of meat in the sieve.
steps.look: About 2 1/2 cups (600 ml) of rich, dark drippings with fat floating on top.
steps.mistake: Skipping the rest, so the juices run out when you cut.
steps.fix: Rest the beef; meanwhile make the gravy.

steps.do: Skim or pour the fat off the drippings. Melt the butter in the saucepan over medium heat, whisk in the flour and cook for 3 to 4 minutes, stirring, until it turns the colour of peanut butter. Gradually whisk in the drippings.
steps.look: A smooth, brown roux that thickens the drippings into a glossy gravy.
steps.mistake: Pouring the drippings in all at once, which makes lumps.
steps.fix: Whisk in gradually; strain if lumps form.

steps.do: Simmer the gravy for 5 minutes until it coats a spoon. Season with hot sauce, salt and pepper.
steps.look: A glossy, brown gravy that coats a spoon.
steps.mistake: Over-reducing, so it turns salty and thick.
steps.fix: Thin with a splash of water or stock.

steps.do: Slice the beef thinly against the grain, then pull apart the ends and scraps into shreds (the debris). Add it all, along with the onion from the sieve, to the gravy and simmer gently for 5 minutes.
steps.look: Tender slices and shreds swimming in rich, glossy gravy.
steps.mistake: Slicing with the grain, which makes long, chewy strands.
steps.fix: Look for the lines in the meat and cut across them.

steps.do: Cut the bread into 6 inch (15 cm) lengths and split each lengthways, leaving a hinge. Warm in the oven at 350°F (175°C) for 2 to 3 minutes.
steps.look: A crackly crust and soft, warm inside.
steps.mistake: Overtoasting, which makes the bread hard and sharp.
steps.fix: Warm it only until the crust crackles.

steps.do: Dress the po' boys: spread both sides of the bread with mayonnaise, pile on beef and debris with plenty of gravy, then lettuce, tomato and pickles. Press closed and cut in half.
steps.look: Gravy soaking into the bread, the filling spilling out, crisp lettuce on top.
steps.mistake: Putting the lettuce under the hot beef, where it wilts.
steps.fix: Hot beef first on the bread, cold vegetables on top.

science: Chuck is a heavily used shoulder muscle with lots of collagen. Roasting it slowly in a covered pot with some liquid at 300°F (150°C) brings the meat up past 190°F (88°C), where collagen steadily converts to gelatin over several hours. That gelatin makes the meat tender and gives the drippings body. The sear at the start builds flavour through the Maillard reaction and leaves fond, which dissolves into the liquid. Resting lets the meat fibres relax and the juices settle, so they are not lost on the board. Cutting against the grain shortens the muscle fibres, making each bite tender. A roux made from butter and flour thickens the drippings into a smooth gravy.
plating: Serve each half po' boy on a sheet of butcher paper or a plate, cut on the diagonal, the cut side facing the guest to show the beef and gravy layer under the crisp lettuce and red tomato. Serve with a pickle spear, crisps or fries and a stack of napkins.

pairing.drink: A cold local lager or amber ale, or a fruity Zinfandel with enough body for beef and gravy.

variations: Shrimp po' boy: cornmeal-fried shrimp with the same dressing.
Roast beef with cheese: add a slice of Swiss cheese melted onto the beef.
Debris only: shred all the beef into the gravy for a sloppier, richer sandwich.

Cool leftover beef and gravy quickly and refrigerate within 2 hours; reheat until steaming, 165°F (74°C).
Use a sharp knife and a steady board; a board slipping on a wet counter is how cuts happen, so put a damp cloth under it.

title: Croquetas de Jamón
summary: Spain's bar staple: a very thick béchamel studded with cured ham, chilled until firm, shaped, crumbed and fried so that a crisp shell gives way to a molten, creamy centre. It pushes the mother sauce to its thickest and adds the full coating and frying sequence.
equipment: Wide heavy saucepan or sauté pan
Balloon whisk and a stiff silicone spatula
Shallow dish or baking tin about 8 by 8 inches (20 by 20 cm)
Cling film
Three shallow bowls for the coating
Heavy pot for frying, at least 4 inches (10 cm) deep
Clip-on deep-fry thermometer
Spider or slotted spoon and a wire rack over a tray

ingredients.item: Jamón serrano or Ibérico, finely chopped

ingredients.note: taste first; the ham is salty

ingredients.item: Olive or sunflower oil for frying

mise: Warm the milk until steaming.
Chop the ham very finely, almost to a mince, with a sharp knife.
Lightly oil the shallow dish.
Set out three bowls for flour, beaten egg and breadcrumbs, and a tray for the coated croquetas.
The béchamel must chill at least 4 hours or overnight, so make it ahead.

timeline.do: Make the thick béchamel, 15 to 20 minutes of stirring; fold in ham.
Spread in the dish, film on the surface, cool and chill at least 4 hours.
Shape into logs; coat flour, egg, crumb, egg, crumb.
Heat the oil to 350 to 375°F (175 to 190°C).
Fry in batches, about 2 minutes each.
Drain on the rack; serve hot.

steps.do: Melt the butter with the olive oil in the wide pan over medium-low heat. If using onion, cook it for 4 minutes until soft and translucent. Add the ham and stir for 1 minute.
steps.look: The ham fat turns translucent and smells sweet and porky.
steps.mistake: Frying the ham until crisp, which makes it hard in the croqueta.
steps.fix: Just warm it through in the butter.

steps.do: Add the flour all at once and stir with the whisk for 3 minutes.
steps.look: A thick paste that bubbles and smells of biscuits, still pale.
steps.mistake: Not cooking the roux long enough, leaving a raw flour taste.
steps.fix: Give it the full 3 minutes.

steps.do: Add the warm milk a ladle at a time, whisking constantly and letting each addition become smooth before adding the next.
steps.look: The paste seizes, then loosens into a smooth, very thick sauce.
steps.mistake: Adding milk too fast, making lumps that are hard to remove from such a thick sauce.
steps.fix: Whisk lumps out before the next ladle; if they persist, briefly use a stick blender.

steps.do: Once all the milk is in, switch to the spatula and cook over low heat for 12 to 15 minutes, stirring constantly and scraping the bottom. Season with nutmeg and salt.
steps.look: The béchamel becomes very thick and glossy and pulls away from the sides of the pan in one mass. A spoon stands up in it briefly.
steps.mistake: Stopping too early, so the béchamel is too soft to shape and the croquetas burst in the oil.
steps.fix: Keep cooking and stirring; it should be almost too thick to stir.

steps.do: Spread the béchamel into the oiled dish, press cling film directly onto the surface, let it cool to room temperature, then refrigerate for at least 4 hours or overnight.
steps.look: A firm, cold, sliceable mass.
steps.mistake: Not covering the surface, so a skin forms.
steps.fix: Film must touch the surface.

steps.do: With lightly oiled hands, scoop about 1 1/2 tbsp (30 g) of the cold mixture and roll it into a small log about 2 inches (5 cm) long. Roll each in flour, then egg, then breadcrumbs, then egg and breadcrumbs again.
steps.look: Neat, evenly coated logs with no bare patches.
steps.mistake: Gaps in the coating, where the filling leaks into the oil.
steps.fix: Double coat thoroughly, pressing the crumbs on.

steps.do: Heat the oil in the heavy pot to 350 to 375°F (175 to 190°C). Fry 4 to 5 croquetas at a time for about 2 minutes, turning once, until deep golden.
steps.look: Vigorous bubbling and an even, deep golden crust.
steps.mistake: Crowding the pot or frying in oil that is too cool, so the croquetas soak up oil and burst.
steps.fix: Small batches, and let the oil return to temperature between them.

steps.do: Lift onto the wire rack with the spider and rest 1 minute before serving.
steps.look: Crisp golden shells; when cut, a creamy, molten centre.
steps.mistake: Serving immediately, so the filling burns mouths.
steps.fix: Rest briefly; the centre is extremely hot.

science: A croqueta filling is a béchamel with far more flour than usual. The starch granules swell and release long starch molecules that tangle into a thick network; cooking it for longer evaporates water and concentrates the starch, so the cooled sauce sets firm enough to shape. Chilling lets the starch molecules re-associate, making it firmer still. When fried, the hot oil sets the coating quickly while the filling inside softens back into a creamy sauce. The double coat of egg and crumb forms a strong barrier: egg proteins set into a seal, and the crumbs fry into a crisp shell. If the oil is too cool, the filling softens before the shell sets and bursts through.
plating: Pile the croquetas in a small pyramid on a warm plate lined with a folded napkin or on a slate board. Add a lemon wedge or a small dish of alioli and serve at once, as a tapa with toothpicks.

pairing.drink: A chilled fino or Manzanilla sherry, whose salty, nutty dryness is the classic Spanish match for jamón and fried food.
pairing.brennans: La Cigarrera Manzanilla Sanlúcar de Barrameda NV (375 ml): a bone-dry, saline sherry made for ham and fried tapas.

variations: Croquetas de pollo: use finely shredded cooked chicken instead of ham.
Croquetas de bacalao: use desalted, flaked salt cod.
Mushroom croquetas: use finely chopped sautéed mushrooms.
safety: Deep frying: fill the pot no more than one third full, use a thermometer, and never leave hot oil unattended.
Never use water on an oil fire; turn off the heat and cover with a lid.
The filling is molten and very hot; warn guests to wait a minute.

title: Cacio e Pepe
summary: Rome's pasta of Pecorino Romano, toasted black pepper and starchy pasta water, emulsified into a creamy sauce with no cream at all. Three ingredients and a sauce that breaks above about 149°F (65°C) make this an exam in emulsions.
skills: a cheese paste emulsified off the heat
equipment: Wide, shallow pot or large deep frying pan for cooking pasta in less water
12 inch (30 cm) skillet
Microplane or fine grater
Mixing bowl
Whisk or fork
Tongs
Heatproof jug
Instant-read thermometer (useful while learning)

ingredients.note: grated on a microplane; pre-grated cheese clumps
less than usual; the cheese is salty
less water makes starchier pasta water

mise: Grate the Pecorino on a microplane into a fluffy pile; it must be fine to melt evenly.
Crack the peppercorns coarsely in a mortar or with the base of a heavy pan.
Put the water on in a wide, shallow pot so the starch is more concentrated.
Have the bowl, whisk, tongs and jug ready beside the stove.

timeline.do: Water on; grate cheese; crack pepper.
Salt the water; pasta in; toast the pepper in the skillet.
Make the cheese paste with warm pasta water.
Pasta into the skillet with pepper and water; take off the heat.
Add the cheese paste and toss to a creamy sauce.
Serve immediately in warm bowls.

steps.do: Toast the cracked pepper in the dry skillet over medium heat for 1 to 2 minutes, shaking, until fragrant. Add a ladle of the pasta water once the pasta is cooking and let it bubble to take up the pepper flavour. Set the pan aside.
steps.look: The pepper smells strongly aromatic and a little smoky.
steps.mistake: Burning the pepper, which turns acrid.
steps.fix: Take it off the heat as soon as it smells; it continues to cook from the pan's heat.

steps.do: Salt the boiling water lightly and add the pasta. Stir for the first minute so it does not stick. Cook for 2 minutes less than the packet says.
steps.look: The water turns milky with starch as the pasta cooks.
steps.mistake: Using a large pot of water, which dilutes the starch.
steps.fix: Use the smaller amount of water and stir often so the pasta does not stick.

steps.do: Meanwhile make the cheese paste: put the Pecorino in the bowl and whisk in about 1/3 cup (80 ml) of pasta water, cooled for a minute in the jug to warm but not boiling, about 140°F (60°C), a little at a time, until it forms a thick, smooth paste.
steps.look: A smooth, creamy paste like thick yoghurt with no lumps.
steps.mistake: Using boiling water, which makes the cheese seize into rubbery clumps straight away.
steps.fix: Let the pasta water cool for a minute first. If it clumps, start again with fresh cheese.

steps.do: Reserve another 1 cup (240 ml) of pasta water. Move the pasta with tongs straight into the skillet with the pepper, add a splash of pasta water and toss over medium heat for 1 minute to finish cooking.
steps.look: The pasta absorbs the peppery liquid and the starch turns the liquid slightly creamy.
steps.mistake: Draining the pasta in a colander and losing the starchy water that clings to it.
steps.fix: Lift with tongs, letting the water cling.

steps.do: Take the skillet off the heat and wait 30 seconds. Add the cheese paste and toss vigorously with tongs, adding pasta water a splash at a time.
steps.look: The paste melts into a smooth, glossy, creamy sauce that coats every strand.
steps.mistake: Adding the cheese over the flame, which overheats it so it breaks into strings and a pool of grease.
steps.fix: If it clumps, add a splash of warm water and toss hard off the heat; if it has fully broken, it cannot be saved, so remember for next time.

steps.do: Keep tossing for 1 minute, loosening with more pasta water until the sauce is creamy and flowing.
steps.look: A loose, glossy sauce, like single cream, clinging to the pasta, with no oily pools.
steps.mistake: Letting it go too thick, so it becomes sticky and gluey as it cools.
steps.fix: It thickens fast; keep it a little looser than you think.

steps.do: Serve immediately in warm bowls with a little more pepper and Pecorino on top.
steps.look: A creamy, glossy nest flecked with black pepper.
steps.mistake: Letting it sit; the sauce sets as it cools.
steps.fix: Plate and eat at once.

science: Cacio e pepe is an emulsion of fat and water held together by starch and cheese proteins. Pecorino's casein proteins are what make it melt smoothly, but above about 149°F (65°C) they tighten and bind to each other, squeezing out fat and forming rubbery clumps. Starch released from the pasta into the water coats the proteins and fat droplets, keeping them apart, so the sauce stays smooth. That is why the cheese is first mixed into a paste with water that is warm, not boiling, and added off the heat: the paste disperses evenly before the proteins can overheat. Toasting black pepper releases its aromatic oils, and its piperine dissolves into the fat.
plating: Use warm, shallow bowls. Lift a portion with tongs, twist it into a neat nest in the centre and spoon any remaining sauce over. Finish with a pinch of coarsely cracked pepper and a fine dusting of Pecorino. Serve at once.

pairing.drink: A crisp Roman white such as Frascati, or a light Verdicchio, whose acidity cuts the salty cheese.

variations: Gricia: add crisp guanciale for the step towards carbonara and amatriciana.
Cacio e pepe with butter: add a tablespoon of butter to the pepper pan for a more forgiving sauce while learning.
Half and half: use half Pecorino and half Parmigiano for a milder, easier sauce.
safety: Carry a pot of boiling water carefully, or lift the pasta out with tongs instead of draining.
Toast pepper away from your face; it can sting the eyes.
