title: Bibimbap
summary: A bowl of warm rice topped with six vegetables, each cooked and seasoned separately, marinated beef, a fried egg and a sweet, spicy gochujang sauce, all mixed together at the table. It builds the habit of tasting and seasoning every component on its own.
equipment: Rice cooker or heavy saucepan with tight lid
Large saucepan of boiling water for blanching
Bowl of iced water and a spider
12 inch (30 cm) frying pan or wok
Nonstick frying pan for the eggs
Several small bowls for the prepared vegetables
Sharp knife and board
Four wide serving bowls, or stone dolsot bowls

ingredients.item: Beef sirloin or rib-eye, thinly sliced
ingredients.note: partly frozen for 20 minutes to slice thin

ingredients.item: Soy sauce, sugar, sesame oil and garlic for the beef
ingredients.us: 1 1/2 tbsp soy, 2 tsp sugar, 1 tsp sesame oil, 1 clove
ingredients.metric: 22 ml soy, 8 g sugar, 5 ml sesame oil, 1 clove

ingredients.item: Toasted sesame oil for the namul
Fine salt and toasted sesame seeds
Sesame oil, sugar, water and rice vinegar for the sauce
ingredients.metric: 15 ml oil, 12 g sugar, 15 ml water, 15 ml vinegar

mise: Rinse and cook the rice; keep it warm.
Slice the beef thinly and marinate it in soy, sugar, sesame oil and garlic for 15 minutes.
Julienne the carrot, courgette and cucumber into matchsticks about 2 inches (5 cm) long; slice the mushrooms.
Salt the courgette and cucumber lightly for 10 minutes, then squeeze dry.
Mix the gochujang sauce.
Bring a large pan of salted water to the boil and set a bowl of iced water beside it.

timeline.do: Cook the rice. Marinate the beef.
Julienne vegetables; salt courgette and cucumber.
Blanch spinach, then sprouts; shock, squeeze, season.
Sauté carrot, courgette, mushrooms in turn; season each.
Stir fry the beef. Mix the sauce.
Fry the eggs. Arrange the bowls.
Serve with sauce; mix at the table.

steps.do: Blanch the spinach in the boiling water for 30 seconds, lift out with the spider into iced water, then squeeze out as much water as possible. Season with 1 tsp (5 ml) sesame oil, a little garlic, a pinch of salt and sesame seeds.
steps.look: Bright green, compact spinach; squeezed into a firm ball.
steps.mistake: Leaving it wet, so it dilutes the seasoning and floods the bowl.
steps.fix: Squeeze firmly with both hands.

steps.do: Blanch the sprouts in the same water for 3 to 4 minutes (soybean) or 1 minute (mung bean), drain, cool slightly and season in the same way.
steps.look: Sprouts tender but still crunchy.
steps.mistake: Undercooking soybean sprouts, which taste raw and beany.
steps.fix: Taste one; cook another minute if beany.

steps.do: Heat 1 tsp (5 ml) neutral oil in the frying pan over medium-high heat and sauté the carrot with a pinch of salt for 1 to 2 minutes until just tender. Move to its own bowl. Wipe the pan.
steps.look: Bright orange, softened but with a little bite.
steps.mistake: Cooking all the vegetables together, so they taste the same.
steps.fix: Cook and season each one alone.

steps.do: Sauté the squeezed courgette for 1 to 2 minutes, then the mushrooms with a little soy sauce for 2 to 3 minutes, each in a little oil, each seasoned and moved to its own bowl. Dress the raw cucumber with a little sesame oil and salt.
steps.look: Each vegetable bright, glossy and individually seasoned.
steps.mistake: Overcooking the courgette to mush.
steps.fix: Cook quickly over high heat.

steps.do: Heat 1 tbsp (15 ml) oil in the pan over high heat and stir fry the beef for 2 to 3 minutes until just browned and cooked through.
steps.look: Caramelised edges, no pink left.
steps.mistake: Crowding the pan so the beef stews.
steps.fix: Cook in two batches.

steps.do: Fry the eggs in the nonstick pan in a little oil over medium heat for 2 to 3 minutes until the whites are set and the yolks runny.
steps.look: Set whites, glossy yolks.
steps.mistake: Frying too hot so the whites go brown and crisp.
steps.fix: Medium heat.

steps.do: Taste each component and adjust its seasoning. Fill each bowl with warm rice. Arrange the vegetables and beef in separate wedges around the bowl like the spokes of a wheel, placing contrasting colours side by side. Put the egg in the centre.
steps.look: A bowl of colourful wedges, with a golden yolk at the centre.
steps.mistake: Piling everything in a heap.
steps.fix: Arrange neatly; the arranged bowl is part of the dish.

steps.do: Serve with the gochujang sauce and sesame seeds on the side. Each person adds sauce to taste and mixes everything together thoroughly before eating.
steps.look: A fully mixed bowl, rice coated in red sauce.
steps.mistake: Not mixing, which misses the point of the dish.
steps.fix: Bibim means mixed; mix it all.

science: Each vegetable has a different water content, texture and cooking time, so cooking and seasoning them separately lets each reach its ideal texture and keeps its own flavour and colour. Blanching briefly in boiling water then shocking in iced water sets the bright green colour of chlorophyll and stops the cooking. Salting courgette and cucumber draws out water by osmosis, so they stay firm and do not dilute the seasoning. Sesame oil carries fat-soluble aromas from garlic and toasted sesame. Gochujang, a fermented chilli paste, contributes heat, sweetness and the deep savoury flavour of fermentation; mixing it through warm rice with the runny yolk creates a light, rich sauce coating every grain.
plating: Use wide bowls. Press warm rice into an even layer. Arrange each vegetable in a neat wedge from the rim to the centre, alternating colours: spinach next to carrot, sprouts next to mushroom, courgette next to beef. Set the egg in the centre, scatter sesame seeds over and serve the sauce in a small dish.

pairing.drink: A light Korean lager or a dry, aromatic white such as Riesling or Grüner Veltliner to balance the chilli.

variations: Dolsot bibimbap: build in a hot stone bowl brushed with sesame oil so the rice forms a crisp crust.
Tofu bibimbap: replace the beef with pan-fried, soy-glazed tofu.
Kimchi bibimbap: add a seventh spoke of chopped kimchi, sautéed for 2 minutes in sesame oil.
safety: Runny yolks: for anyone vulnerable, use pasteurised eggs or cook the yolk until firm.
Cooked rice should not sit warm for long; serve within two hours or chill quickly.
Bean sprouts are eaten cooked here; blanch them fully.

title: Pad Thai
summary: Rice noodles stir fried with shrimp, tofu, egg and a tamarind, fish sauce and palm sugar sauce, finished with bean sprouts, garlic chives, peanuts and lime. It is an exercise in mise en place and batch size, because a crowded wok steams instead of frying.
skills: a tamarind, fish sauce and palm sugar sauce
cooking in batches in a hot wok
equipment: Carbon steel wok or a 12 inch (30 cm) heavy frying pan
Wok spatula or wide metal spatula
Large bowl for soaking noodles
Small saucepan for the sauce
Colander
Small bowls for every ingredient, lined up in order
Sharp knife and board

ingredients.item: Dried flat rice noodles, about 1/8 inch (3 to 5 mm) wide

ingredients.note: or soak 1 1/2 oz (40 g) tamarind pulp in warm water and strain
cut in small cubes and patted dry

ingredients.item: Garlic chives, cut in 1 1/2 inch (4 cm) lengths

mise: Soak the noodles in room temperature water for 45 minutes to 1 hour (or warm water for 30 minutes) until pliable but still firm. Drain well.
Make the sauce: heat the tamarind, fish sauce and palm sugar gently in the small pan, stirring until the sugar dissolves, about 2 minutes. Taste: it should be sour, sweet and salty in equal measure.
Peel and devein the shrimp, cube and dry the tofu, slice the shallots, mince the garlic.
Line up every ingredient in small bowls beside the wok in the order they go in: oil, tofu, shrimp, shallot and garlic, dried shrimp and radish, noodles, sauce, eggs, sprouts and chives.
Divide everything in half if cooking for four; you will cook two batches.

timeline.do: Soak the noodles.
Make the sauce; prep and line up everything in order.
Cook batch one, about 4 minutes.
Wipe the wok; cook batch two.
Peanuts, lime and chilli at the table.

steps.do: Heat the wok over high heat until it just smokes, then add 2 tbsp (30 ml) oil and swirl. Add the tofu and fry for 1 to 2 minutes until golden on several sides.
steps.look: The oil shimmers and the tofu sizzles loudly and turns golden.
steps.mistake: A wok that is not hot enough, so the tofu sticks and the dish steams.
steps.fix: Heat the wok longer before the oil goes in.

steps.do: Add the shrimp and cook for 1 minute per side until pink, then add the shallots, garlic, dried shrimp and radish and stir for 30 seconds.
steps.look: Pink, curled shrimp and fragrant, lightly golden garlic.
steps.mistake: Burning the garlic.
steps.fix: Keep everything moving; the garlic needs only 30 seconds.

steps.do: Add the drained noodles and half the sauce and toss continuously with the spatula for 1 to 2 minutes. Add the rest of the sauce gradually as the noodles absorb it, and a splash of water if they look dry and stiff.
steps.look: The noodles turn soft, glossy and translucent, coated in a brown sauce.
steps.mistake: Boiled or over-soaked noodles, which break into mush in the wok.
steps.fix: Soak only until pliable; they finish cooking in the sauce.

steps.do: Push the noodles to one side, add 1 tbsp (15 ml) oil to the empty space, crack in an egg and scramble it until half set. Fold the noodles over it and toss to mix.
steps.look: Soft curds of egg through the noodles.
steps.mistake: Pouring the egg over the noodles, where it coats them in a gluey layer.
steps.fix: Cook the egg in the cleared space first.

steps.do: Add half the bean sprouts and chives and toss for 30 seconds. Taste and adjust with a splash of fish sauce or sugar.
steps.look: Sprouts and chives just wilted but still crisp.
steps.mistake: Cooking the sprouts until limp and watery.
steps.fix: They go in at the very end.

steps.do: Tip onto a warm plate. Wipe the wok, and repeat with the second batch if cooking for four.
steps.look: Glossy, separate noodles with no liquid pooling on the plate.
steps.mistake: Cooking all four portions at once, so the wok cools and the noodles stew.
steps.fix: Always cook in batches of two portions.

steps.do: Top with peanuts and serve with lime wedges, the remaining sprouts and chilli flakes on the side.
steps.look: A neat heap of noodles with a lime wedge and peanuts.
steps.mistake: Adding peanuts in the wok, where they go soft.
steps.fix: Peanuts go on at the end.

science: Rice noodles are made of rice starch with no gluten. Soaking in water rehydrates them so the starch softens, while leaving them firm enough to finish cooking in the wok. Boiled noodles have already absorbed too much water and swollen starch, so they break and turn mushy when tossed. A very hot wok evaporates liquid quickly so the noodles fry and caramelise rather than stew, and the high heat develops the smoky flavour from the Maillard reaction and caramelisation of the sauce's sugars. A crowded wok loses heat rapidly, releasing steam. The sauce balances three tastes: sour tamarind from tartaric acid, sweet palm sugar and salty, savoury fish sauce rich in glutamates.
plating: Mound the noodles high in the centre of a warm plate, with shrimp tucked visibly into the top. Sprinkle peanuts over, and place a lime wedge, a small pile of raw bean sprouts and a few lengths of garlic chive to one side. Add a small dish of chilli flakes and sugar for guests to adjust.

pairing.drink: An off-dry Riesling or Gewürztraminer; the touch of sweetness and acidity balance tamarind, fish sauce and chilli.
pairing.brennans: Trimbach Riesling Réserve 2020: a crisp, aromatic Alsace Riesling with the acidity to match tamarind and lime.

variations: Chicken pad Thai: replace the shrimp with thinly sliced chicken thigh, cooked through.
Vegetarian: replace fish sauce with soy sauce and leave out the shrimp.
Pad Thai wrapped in egg: wrap the noodles in a thin omelette, as some street vendors do.
safety: A smoking hot wok and oil can flare; keep a lid nearby and never leave the wok.
Cook shrimp until pink and opaque, 145°F (63°C).
If serving to guests, name the peanuts, egg, fish sauce and shrimp in the dish so they can ask about them.

title: Bánh Mì Thịt
summary: The full Vietnamese sandwich: a crisp, light roll spread with home-made chicken liver pâté and mayonnaise, filled with roast lemongrass pork, quick-pickled carrot and daikon, cucumber, coriander and chilli. It adds roasting and a simple pâté to the breakfast lesson, and teaches the contrast that makes a great sandwich.
equipment: Roasting tin with a rack
Mixing bowls for the marinade and pickles
Mortar and pestle or small food processor
Frying pan and a blender for the pâté
Small ramekin and cling film
Instant-read thermometer
Mandoline or sharp knife for julienne
Bread knife

ingredients.item: Pork shoulder or pork belly, boneless
ingredients.note: in one piece, or 2 slabs about 1 inch (2.5 cm) thick

ingredients.item: Lemongrass stalks, tender inner part, minced
Rice vinegar, warm water, sugar and salt for pickles
ingredients.us: 1/2 cup vinegar, 1/2 cup water, 3 tbsp sugar, 1 tsp salt
ingredients.metric: 120 ml vinegar, 120 ml water, 40 g sugar, 6 g salt

ingredients.note: trimmed of sinew and green spots

ingredients.item: Butter, shallot and garlic for pâté
Brandy or fish sauce for pâté

mise: Make the marinade: pound the lemongrass, shallots and garlic, then mix with fish sauce, sugar, oil and pepper. Coat the pork and marinate at least 1 hour, or overnight in the fridge.
Make the pickles: dissolve the sugar and salt in the warm water, add the vinegar, then the julienned carrot and daikon. Leave at least 30 minutes.
Trim the chicken livers: cut away any connecting sinew and any green-stained patches, which are bitter.
Cut the cucumber into spears, pick the coriander sprigs, slice the chilli.

timeline.do: Marinate the pork; make the pickles.
Make the pâté; chill at least 1 hour.
Oven to 375°F (190°C). Roast the pork 45 to 60 minutes.
Rest the pork 10 minutes; slice thin.
Warm the rolls; prepare garnishes.
Build and serve.

steps.do: For the pâté, melt 1 tbsp (14 g) butter in the frying pan over medium heat, cook the shallot and garlic for 2 minutes, then add the livers and cook for 2 to 3 minutes a side.
steps.look: Browned outside; cut open, the livers are firm and no longer pink in the centre.
steps.mistake: Leaving the livers pink inside.
steps.fix: Chicken livers must reach 165°F (74°C); check with a thermometer or cut one open.

steps.do: Add the brandy or fish sauce and let it bubble off. Blend the livers with the remaining butter, softened, and a pinch of salt and pepper until very smooth. Press into a ramekin, cover the surface with cling film and chill for at least 1 hour.
steps.look: A smooth, glossy, pinkish-brown pâté that sets firm when chilled.
steps.mistake: A grainy pâté from overcooked livers or underblending.
steps.fix: Blend longer, then push through a sieve for extra smoothness.

steps.do: Heat the oven to 375°F (190°C). Place the marinated pork on the rack in the roasting tin and roast for 45 to 60 minutes, turning once.
steps.look: Caramelised, dark edges where the sugar in the marinade has browned. The centre reads 145°F (63°C) for sliceable shoulder, or higher for belly.
steps.mistake: Roasting at too high a heat, so the sugar burns black before the pork is cooked.
steps.fix: Cover loosely with foil if browning too quickly.

steps.do: For extra colour, put the pork under a hot overhead grill (broiler) for 2 to 3 minutes. Rest for 10 minutes, then slice very thinly.
steps.look: Sticky, caramelised edges and juicy, thin slices.
steps.mistake: Slicing straight away, so the juices run out.
steps.fix: Rest it first.

steps.do: Warm the rolls in the oven for 3 to 4 minutes until the crust crackles. Split them along one side, leaving a hinge, and pull out a little of the soft crumb.
steps.look: A crisp, hollow shell with a light, soft interior.
steps.mistake: Overtoasting, so the crust shatters into sharp pieces.
steps.fix: Just warm until it crackles.

steps.do: Spread one side with pâté and the other with mayonnaise. Layer in the pork, then drained pickles, cucumber spears, coriander sprigs and chilli. Add a few dashes of Maggi.
steps.look: A full sandwich, colourful and stuffed.
steps.mistake: Undrained pickles, which soak the bread.
steps.fix: Squeeze the pickles lightly first.

steps.do: Press the sandwich closed and serve at once.
steps.look: Crisp bread, rich pâté, sticky pork and sharp pickles.
steps.mistake: Building them ahead, so the bread goes soggy.
steps.fix: Assemble just before eating.

science: The marinade combines fish sauce and sugar: salt in the fish sauce seasons the meat and helps it hold moisture, and the sugar caramelises in the oven to give the sticky, browned edges. Lemongrass carries citrus aroma compounds that are released by pounding. The quick pickle uses vinegar's acid and salt to draw water from the carrot and daikon by osmosis, keeping them crunchy while adding a sweet and sour flavour. Chicken liver pâté is an emulsion of cooked liver and butter. Liver proteins become grainy if overcooked, so they are cooked just to a safe temperature and blended while warm so the butter emulsifies smoothly. The contrasts of crisp, soft, rich, sour and hot make the sandwich.
plating: Cut each bánh mì in half on the diagonal and serve on a board or paper, cut sides facing up to show the layers: pâté, pork, orange and white pickles, green cucumber and coriander. Add a small dish of extra chilli and pickles.

pairing.drink: A Vietnamese iced coffee, or a crisp lager or dry Riesling to refresh after the rich pâté and pork.

variations: Bánh mì gà: grilled lemongrass chicken thighs instead of pork.
Bánh mì xíu mại: meatballs in tomato sauce.
Vegetarian: lemongrass tofu and a mushroom pâté.
safety: Chicken livers must reach 165°F (74°C); undercooked liver is a known source of food poisoning.
Pork must reach 145°F (63°C) with a 3 minute rest.
Keep the pâté refrigerated and eat it within 3 days.

title: Tacos de Carnitas
summary: Pork shoulder cooked slowly in lard with orange, garlic and spices until it falls apart, then crisped in its own fat and served in warm corn tortillas with a raw tomatillo salsa verde. It is confit in a Mexican accent, and teaches gentle cooking in fat followed by a hard crisping.
skills: slow cooking pork in lard with orange
equipment: Heavy 5 to 6 quart (5 to 6 litre) Dutch oven
Instant-read thermometer
Slotted spoon and tongs
Rimmed baking tray (for crisping) or a large cast iron pan
Blender for the salsa
Comal, griddle or dry frying pan for tortillas
Clean tea towel or tortilla warmer

ingredients.note: cut in 2 inch (5 cm) chunks, fat left on
or enough to come halfway up the pork; part neutral oil is fine

ingredients.item: Bay leaves, dried oregano and cinnamon stick
Serrano chilli, garlic, onion and coriander for salsa
ingredients.metric: 1 chilli, 1 clove, about 40 g onion, 15 g coriander

ingredients.item: White onion and coriander to finish

mise: Cut the pork into even 2 inch (5 cm) chunks and toss with the salt. Leave for 30 minutes, or overnight in the fridge.
Heat the oven to 300°F (150°C) if cooking in the oven.
Halve the orange; smash the garlic.
Make the salsa verde cruda (step 7) while the pork cooks; it is best within a few hours.
Chop the onion and coriander for finishing; cut the limes.

timeline.do: Salt the pork.
Pork, lard, orange, onion, garlic and spices in the pot; bring to a gentle bubble.
Cook gently 2 1/2 hours, stovetop very low or oven at 300°F (150°C).
Lift out the pork; rest; make the salsa.
Crisp the pork in a hot pan with some of its fat.
Warm the tortillas.
Build tacos with salsa, onion, coriander and lime.

steps.do: Melt the lard in the Dutch oven over medium heat. Add the pork in a snug single layer; it should come about halfway up the pieces. Squeeze in the orange juice and drop in the orange halves, onion, garlic, bay, oregano and cinnamon. Add the milk if using.
steps.look: The fat melts and begins to bubble gently around the meat.
steps.mistake: Using too little fat, so the pork fries rather than poaches.
steps.fix: Add more lard or oil to come at least halfway up.

steps.do: Bring to a gentle bubble, then lower the heat to the lowest setting (or move to the 300°F (150°C) oven) and cook for 2 to 2 1/2 hours, turning the pieces every 30 minutes. The fat should bubble slowly, never fry hard.
steps.look: Small, lazy bubbles around the meat; the fat stays clear. The pork turns pale gold and then begins to brown.
steps.mistake: Frying the pork at high heat, which makes it tough and dry.
steps.fix: If it is spitting and browning fast, lower the heat; the fat should sit around 200 to 250°F (95 to 120°C).

steps.do: Test the pork: a piece should fall apart when pressed with tongs.
steps.look: Tender, golden, glistening chunks that collapse at a touch.
steps.mistake: Pulling it while still firm.
steps.fix: Cook in 20 minute stages until tender.

steps.do: Lift the pork onto a tray with the slotted spoon and let it cool for 10 minutes. Strain and keep the fat. Discard the orange, onion and spices.
steps.look: Juicy, tender pork; clear, flavourful fat.
steps.mistake: Throwing away the fat, which is full of flavour and good for crisping.
steps.fix: Keep it in a jar in the fridge for weeks.

steps.do: Pull the pork into large chunks and shreds with two forks.
steps.look: A mix of large pieces and shreds, with plenty of edges to crisp.
steps.mistake: Shredding finely, which dries out.
steps.fix: Leave plenty of large pieces.

steps.do: Heat 3 tbsp (45 ml) of the strained fat in a large cast iron pan over medium-high heat. Add the pork in one layer and leave it for 3 to 4 minutes, then turn and crisp for 2 to 3 minutes more. Work in batches.
steps.look: Deep golden, crackling edges on the outside, while the inside stays moist.
steps.mistake: Stirring constantly, so the pork never crisps.
steps.fix: Leave it still to build a crust.

steps.do: For the salsa verde cruda, blend the raw tomatillos, chilli, garlic, onion, coriander, lime juice and a pinch of salt with 2 tbsp (30 ml) water until fairly smooth. Taste for salt and sharpness.
steps.look: A bright green, tangy, slightly loose salsa.
steps.mistake: Blending until frothy and pale.
steps.fix: Pulse to keep some texture; let it settle before serving.

steps.do: Warm the tortillas on a hot dry comal for 30 seconds a side until soft and lightly spotted, and stack them in a tea towel.
steps.look: Soft, pliable tortillas with a few toasted spots.
steps.mistake: Cold tortillas, which crack when folded.
steps.fix: Warm each one and keep them wrapped.

steps.do: Build tacos: two tortillas stacked per taco, a pile of carnitas, a spoon of salsa, chopped onion and coriander, and lime on the side.
steps.look: Crisp golden pork, bright green salsa and white onion on soft tortillas.
steps.mistake: Overfilling, so the taco falls apart.
steps.fix: A modest pile per taco; serve more tacos instead.

science: Cooking pork shoulder slowly submerged in fat is a confit: fat transfers heat gently and evenly and, unlike water, does not dissolve the meat's juices away. Held well below frying temperature, the abundant collagen in the shoulder slowly melts into gelatin, so the meat becomes tender and moist. Orange juice adds acid and sugar, and milk adds proteins and lactose, both of which help the pork brown. Once tender, the pork is crisped at much higher heat, so the surface dries and browns quickly through the Maillard reaction while the inside stays juicy. Salting ahead seasons the meat throughout. Tomatillos in the raw salsa are naturally acidic and full of pectin, giving body and brightness.
plating: Serve three tacos per person on a warm plate or a wooden board, slightly overlapping, with the pork piled high and the salsa spooned over in a stripe. Add onion and coriander on top, two lime wedges on the side and extra salsa in a small dish.

pairing.drink: A Mexican lager with lime, or a fresh margarita, whose lime cuts through the pork fat.

variations: Oven carnitas: braise in a little lard and orange juice in a covered dish at 300°F (150°C), then crisp under the overhead grill (broiler).
Carnitas with pickled onions: serve with red onions pickled in lime juice.
Torta de carnitas: pile into a toasted bolillo roll with beans and avocado.
safety: Hot fat: use a heavy pot no more than half full, lower meat in gently, and never leave it on high heat.
Pork must reach 145°F (63°C) with a rest; slow-cooked carnitas are far beyond this.
Let the fat cool completely before straining and storing.

title: Falafel in Pita with Tahini Sauce
summary: Crisp green-centred falafel made from soaked, uncooked chickpeas ground with herbs, onion and spices, fried and stuffed into pita with salad, pickles and tahini sauce. It teaches why soaked raw chickpeas hold together and canned ones fall apart, and adds a second deep fry with tighter control.
equipment: Large bowl for soaking
Food processor (a blender will not work)
Heavy pot at least 4 inches (10 cm) deep
Clip-on deep-fry thermometer
Falafel scoop or two spoons
Spider and a wire rack over a tray
Small bowl and whisk for the tahini sauce

ingredients.item: Flat-leaf parsley, leaves and tender stems
Garlic clove for sauce and cold water
Tomato, cucumber, red onion, lettuce and pickled turnip or cucumber

mise: Soak the chickpeas in plenty of cold water for 18 to 24 hours; they will more than double. Drain and dry them well on a towel.
Wash and dry the herbs thoroughly; wet herbs make the mixture loose.
Make the tahini sauce in advance (step 7).
Chop the salad vegetables and set out the pickles.
Set up the fryer: pot no more than one third full, thermometer, rack over a tray, spider and a lid nearby.

timeline.do: Soak the dried chickpeas.
Drain and dry the chickpeas; grind with herbs and spices.
Rest the mixture 30 minutes in the fridge. Make the tahini sauce.
Heat oil to 350°F (175°C); stir in baking powder; shape.
Fry in batches 3 to 4 minutes each.
Warm pita; fill and serve.

steps.do: Put the drained chickpeas, onion and garlic in the food processor and pulse 15 to 20 times, scraping down the sides.
steps.look: A coarse mixture like breadcrumbs.
steps.mistake: Using canned or cooked chickpeas, which make a wet paste that falls apart in the oil.
steps.fix: There is no fix for cooked chickpeas; start again with dried ones.

steps.do: Add the herbs, spices and salt and pulse until the mixture is like coarse couscous and bright green, and holds together when squeezed in your hand.
steps.look: A speckled green mixture that clumps when pressed.
steps.mistake: Processing to a smooth paste, which gives dense, heavy falafel.
steps.fix: Stop at a couscous texture; if it does not hold, pulse a few more times.

steps.do: Transfer to a bowl, cover and refrigerate for 30 minutes.
steps.look: The mixture firms up slightly.
steps.mistake: Skipping the rest, so the falafel crumble.
steps.fix: Rest it; the starches hydrate and bind.

steps.do: Heat the oil to 350°F (175°C). Stir the baking powder into the mixture. Test one: squeeze a tablespoon into a ball or patty and fry it.
steps.look: The test falafel holds its shape and browns evenly.
steps.mistake: Skipping the test, then losing a whole batch to the oil.
steps.fix: If it falls apart, mix in flour 1 tbsp (8 g) at a time and test again.

steps.do: Shape the mixture into balls or patties about 1 1/2 inches (4 cm) across with a scoop or wet hands, without packing them too tightly.
steps.look: Firm but not compressed shapes.
steps.mistake: Packing hard, which makes dense falafel.
steps.fix: Squeeze just enough to hold together.

steps.do: Fry 5 or 6 at a time for 3 to 4 minutes, turning once, until deep brown. Lift onto the rack.
steps.look: Deep golden brown crust and a bright green, fluffy, cooked interior when broken open.
steps.mistake: Oil too hot, browning the outside before the inside cooks; or too cool, so they absorb oil.
steps.fix: Hold the oil at 350°F (175°C); adjust the heat between batches.

steps.do: For the tahini sauce, whisk the tahini, lemon juice, grated garlic and a pinch of salt. It will thicken and seize. Whisk in cold water a tablespoon at a time until smooth and pourable.
steps.look: A smooth, pale, creamy sauce like single cream.
steps.mistake: Panicking when it seizes and goes thick; that is normal.
steps.fix: Keep adding water and whisking; it will loosen.

steps.do: Warm the pita and split it open. Fill with salad, 3 or 4 falafel lightly crushed, pickles and plenty of tahini sauce.
steps.look: A full pita with crisp falafel, fresh salad and dripping sauce.
steps.mistake: Assembling too early so the pita goes soggy.
steps.fix: Build just before eating.

science: Soaked raw chickpeas are full of uncooked starch and protein. When ground and fried, that starch gelatinises and the proteins set, binding the falafel as it cooks. Cooked or canned chickpeas have already gelatinised their starch and absorbed lots of water, so they make a wet paste; in the oil that water turns to steam and blows the falafel apart. Grinding coarsely leaves air pockets that keep the inside light. Baking powder releases carbon dioxide when heated, adding lift. Tahini seizes when water is first added because the ground sesame particles absorb water and clump; adding more water dilutes them into a smooth emulsion, with the lemon juice adding sharpness.
plating: Serve the pita upright in a paper sleeve or on a plate, open end up, with falafel peeping out. Or plate open: a pool of tahini sauce on the plate, four falafel on top, a chopped salad and pickles alongside, and warm pita cut into triangles.

pairing.drink: A fresh mint lemonade, or a dry Provençal rosé whose fruit and acidity suit herbs and tahini.

variations: Egyptian ta'ameya: use dried split fava beans instead of chickpeas.
Baked falafel: brush with oil and bake at 400°F (200°C) for 20 minutes, turning halfway; less crisp but simple.
Falafel plate: serve with hummus, tabbouleh and pickles instead of pita.
safety: Deep frying: use a thermometer, fill the pot no more than one third full, lower falafel in gently, and never leave hot oil unattended.
Never put water on an oil fire; turn off the heat and cover with a lid.
Never eat the soaked chickpeas raw; they must be fully fried.

title: Moin Moin
summary: A silky, savoury steamed pudding of peeled black-eyed beans blended with red pepper, onion and Scotch bonnet, enriched with oil and cooked in leaves or moulds. It uses the akara purée in an entirely different way, and teaches steaming and how to test a set.
equipment: Large bowl for soaking and skinning
Blender
Large pot with a lid and a steamer rack, or a wide pan for a water bath
Ramekins, heatproof cups or foil cases (8), or banana leaves
Ladle
Skewer or thin knife
Oven gloves

ingredients.note: palm oil gives the traditional colour

ingredients.item: Cooked flaked fish or corned beef

mise: Soak the beans for 1 to 2 hours in warm water.
Skin the beans by rubbing and floating off the skins, as for akara, until they are clean and white.
Oil the ramekins or cups well.
Set up the steamer: water in the pot below the rack, lid ready. If using a water bath, use a wide pan with water halfway up the cups.
Boil and quarter the eggs; flake the fish.

timeline.do: Soak the beans.
Skin the beans.
Blend with pepper, onion and chilli; season; add oil.
Fill cups, add egg and fish, cover and steam 45 to 50 minutes.
Test with a skewer; rest 5 minutes.
Turn out or serve in the cups.

steps.do: Blend the skinned beans, red pepper, onion and Scotch bonnet with about 1/2 cup (120 ml) of the warm stock until completely smooth, 2 to 3 minutes, scraping down as needed.
steps.look: A very smooth, pale orange batter with no grit when rubbed between your fingers.
steps.mistake: A gritty batter, which gives a coarse, crumbly moin moin.
steps.fix: Blend longer; add a little more liquid if the blender struggles.

steps.do: Pour into a bowl, crumble in the stock cube, add the salt and the oil and whisk for 2 to 3 minutes to aerate. Add more warm stock until the batter is like a thick pancake batter.
steps.look: A smooth, slightly airy batter that pours slowly from the ladle, turned orange by the oil.
steps.mistake: Too thick a batter, which gives a dense, dry moin moin; too thin, which will not set.
steps.fix: Add the stock a spoonful at a time near the end, because a thin batter cannot be thickened; if it has gone too thin, steam it 10 to 15 minutes longer and expect a softer set.

steps.do: Taste a little of the batter on the tip of a spoon for salt and heat, then spit it out. Adjust seasoning.
steps.look: Well seasoned and peppery.
steps.mistake: Under-seasoning, which makes it bland once steamed.
steps.fix: Season boldly; steaming mutes flavour.

steps.do: Fill the oiled cups three quarters full. Tuck a piece of egg and some fish into each. Cover each cup tightly with foil.
steps.look: Cups filled to three quarters, with the egg submerged.
steps.mistake: Overfilling, so the moin moin spills as it rises.
steps.fix: Leave room for it to swell.

steps.do: Place on the rack over simmering water, cover the pot with a tight lid and steam over medium heat for 45 to 50 minutes. Check the water every 15 minutes and top up with boiling water.
steps.look: Steady steam escaping under the lid.
steps.mistake: Letting the pot boil dry.
steps.fix: Keep a kettle of hot water ready to top up.

steps.do: Test one: insert a skewer into the centre.
steps.look: The moin moin is firm and springy, like a set custard, and the skewer comes out clean.
steps.mistake: Pulling it while still wet in the centre.
steps.fix: Steam 10 minutes more and test again.

steps.do: Lift out with oven gloves and rest for 5 minutes. Run a knife round the edge and turn out onto plates, or serve in the cups.
steps.look: A smooth, orange, sliceable pudding with egg inside.
steps.mistake: Turning out too soon, so it breaks.
steps.fix: Rest first.

science: Skinned black-eyed beans contain protein and starch that behave much like an egg custard when blended smooth and cooked gently. As the batter is steamed, the starch gelatinises and the proteins coagulate, setting the batter into a soft, sliceable pudding. Steaming cooks at about 212°F (100°C) with moist heat, so the outside does not dry out or brown before the centre sets. Whisking air into the batter makes the texture lighter. Oil coats the proteins and starch, making the texture silky rather than rubbery, and palm oil adds its characteristic colour and flavour. A smooth blend matters because coarse pieces of bean stop the batter setting evenly.
plating: Turn out each moin moin onto a warm plate, sliced in half to show the egg inside, or serve in its leaf, unwrapped at the table. Pair with jollof rice, fried plantain, or pap, with a spoon of pepper sauce on the side.

pairing.drink: A Chapman or a cold ginger beer to refresh after the pepper.

variations: Leaf-wrapped: fold banana leaves into cones, fill and tie, for the traditional perfume.
Moin moin elemi meje: the rich version with egg, fish and corned beef.
Vegetarian: leave out the fish and use vegetable stock.
safety: Steam burns quickly; open the lid away from your face and use oven gloves to lift the cups.
Keep the steamer topped up so it never boils dry.
Cool leftovers quickly and refrigerate; reheat by steaming until hot through.

title: Amritsari Chole with Bhature
summary: Dark, tangy chickpeas boiled with tea and whole spices, then cooked in a deeply browned onion and tomato masala, served with bhature, a yoghurt-leavened dough fried until it balloons. It deepens the chickpea masala from the Commis course and adds a dough that puffs in hot oil.

ingredients.item: Black cardamom, cassia, cloves and bay leaves

ingredients.note: half pounded to a paste, half in julienne

ingredients.item: Garlic cloves, pounded to a paste
Amchur, ground coriander, Kashmiri chilli powder
Kala namak (black salt) and roasted cumin
Baking powder and bicarbonate of soda for bhature
Sugar, salt and oil for the dough
ingredients.us: 1 tsp sugar, 1/2 tsp salt, 1 tbsp oil
ingredients.metric: 4 g sugar, 3 g salt, 15 ml oil

mise: Soak the chickpeas 8 hours or overnight in 6 cups (1.5 litres) cold water with the bicarbonate of soda.
Tie the tea in a muslin bag.
Slice the onions, chop the tomatoes, pound the garlic and half the ginger, julienne the rest.
Measure the ground spices into a small bowl.
Make the bhature dough at least 2 hours before frying (step 6).

timeline.do: Soak chickpeas with bicarbonate.
Boil chickpeas with tea and whole spices, 45 to 60 minutes.
Make bhature dough; rest 2 hours covered.
Brown onions 15 minutes; ginger and garlic; spices off the heat; tomatoes 12 minutes.
Add chickpeas and liquor; simmer 15 minutes; mash some to thicken.
Heat frying oil; roll and fry bhature one at a time.
Finish chole; serve with hot bhature, onion and lemon.

steps.do: Drain the chickpeas, put them in the pot with fresh water to cover by 2 inches (5 cm), the tea bag, whole spices and 1 tsp (6 g) salt. Boil for 45 to 60 minutes (or 15 minutes at pressure) until completely tender. Remove the tea bag and whole spices.
steps.look: The chickpeas are stained dark brown and crush to a smooth paste between your fingers. The liquor is almost black.
steps.mistake: Undercooked chickpeas, which stay firm and never absorb the masala.
steps.fix: Keep cooking until they crush easily; top up the water as needed.

steps.do: Heat the ghee in the frying pan over medium heat and brown the onions for 15 minutes, stirring often.
steps.look: The onions collapse and turn a deep reddish brown, the colour of an old penny, and smell sweet.
steps.mistake: Pale onions, which give a thin, sweetish gravy without depth.
steps.fix: Keep going; dark brown onions give the colour and depth of Amritsari chole.

steps.do: Add the ginger and garlic paste and stir for 1 to 2 minutes until the raw smell becomes sweet. Take the pan off the heat. Add the ground coriander, chilli, anardana and amchur, and stir in a spoonful of the chickpea liquor to wet them.
steps.look: A thick, dark paste that smells toasty, not burnt.
steps.mistake: Adding ground spices over a hot flame, so they scorch and turn bitter.
steps.fix: Off the heat, wetted with liquid, then back on.

steps.do: Return to medium heat, add the tomatoes and a pinch of salt and cook, stirring, for 12 minutes, until the masala pulls away from the sides in one mass and the ghee separates at the edges.
steps.look: A thick, glossy, dark masala with oil gleaming at the rim.
steps.mistake: Stopping before the oil separates, so the gravy tastes raw.
steps.fix: Keep cooking and stirring; add a splash of liquor if it catches.

steps.do: Add the chickpeas and 1 1/4 cups (300 ml) of their liquor. Simmer for 15 minutes. Mash a ladleful against the side of the pan and stir it in to thicken. Finish with kala namak, roasted cumin, remaining salt to taste, ginger julienne and slit chillies.
steps.look: A thick, dark brown gravy clinging to the chickpeas, tangy and spicy.
steps.mistake: A watery gravy.
steps.fix: Simmer longer and mash more chickpeas.

steps.do: For the bhature, mix the flour, semolina, baking powder, bicarbonate, sugar and salt. Add the yoghurt and oil and mix, then add warm water a little at a time and knead 8 minutes to a soft, smooth dough. Cover and rest 2 hours.
steps.look: A soft, smooth, slightly springy dough.
steps.mistake: A stiff dough, which will not puff.
steps.fix: Knead in more water; the dough should be soft.

steps.do: Heat the frying oil to 375°F (190°C). Divide the dough into 8 balls. Roll one into an oval about 6 inches (15 cm) long and 1/8 inch (3 mm) thick, using a little oil rather than flour on the board.
steps.look: An even oval, not too thin.
steps.mistake: Uneven thickness, so the bhatura puffs only in places.
steps.fix: Roll evenly from the centre, turning often.

steps.do: Slide the bhatura gently into the oil. As it rises, press it gently with the back of the slotted spoon so it balloons. Fry 30 to 40 seconds, flip and fry 20 to 30 seconds more.
steps.look: The bhatura puffs dramatically into a golden balloon with pale spots.
steps.mistake: Oil too cool, so the bhatura stays flat and absorbs oil.
steps.fix: Wait for the oil to reach 375°F (190°C) and come back up between each one.

steps.do: Lift onto the rack and serve immediately with the chole, sliced onion, pickle and lemon wedges.
steps.look: A puffed golden bhatura beside a bowl of dark chole.
steps.mistake: Holding the bhature; they deflate and turn leathery.
steps.fix: Fry them as the table is ready to eat.

science: Bicarbonate of soda makes the soaking water alkaline, which weakens the pectin holding the chickpea cell walls together, so they cook to a creamy softness. Ground spices have a large surface area and scorch fast in hot fat, which is why they are added off the heat and wetted. Bhature rise because the yoghurt's lactic acid reacts with bicarbonate and baking powder, producing gas, while resting lets the dough ferment slightly. In very hot oil, water in the dough flashes to steam and inflates it like a balloon before the crust sets.
plating: Serve the chole in a warm bowl, topped with ginger julienne, a slit green chilli and a sprinkle of roasted cumin. Set two puffed bhature on a plate beside it, with sliced red onion, lemon wedges and a spoonful of mango pickle.

pairing.drink: A salted or sweet lassi, which cools the spice, or a cold lager.

variations: Chole kulche: serve with soft, leavened kulcha flatbreads instead of bhature.
Pindi chole: a drier, darker version with more anardana and no tomato.
With puri: smaller, unleavened whole wheat puffed breads instead of bhature.
safety: Deep frying: fill the pot no more than one third full, use a thermometer, slide the dough in away from you, and never leave the oil.
Keep water and wet hands away from the hot oil.
If using a pressure cooker, follow its instructions and let the pressure release fully before opening.

title: Kitsune Udon with Hand-Made Noodles

Large pot for boiling, at least 6 quarts (6 litres)

Saucepans for the broth and the tofu
Potato starch or cornflour for dusting

ingredients.item: Plain flour (medium protein, or udon flour)

ingredients.note: home-made kombu and bonito, or kombu and shiitake for vegetarian

ingredients.item: Dashi, soy, mirin and sugar for the tofu
ingredients.us: 3/4 cup dashi, 2 tbsp each soy, mirin and sugar

mise: Dissolve the salt completely in the cold water.
Make the dashi if you do not have it; keep it hot.
Pour boiling water over the aburaage and drain to remove excess oil; squeeze gently and cut each in half.
Slice the spring onions and kamaboko.
Clear a large work surface for rolling.

Knead by foot in a bag, fold, repeat 3 times; rest 2 hours.
Simmer the aburaage 10 to 15 minutes; leave in its syrup.
Roll and cut the noodles.
Make the broth; bring the noodle water to a rolling boil.

Noodles in bowls; hot broth; tofu, spring onion, shichimi.

steps.do: Put the flour in the bowl and add the salted water a little at a time, rubbing it in with your fingertips until the flour is crumbly like coarse breadcrumbs. Then press it together into a rough, firm ball.
steps.look: A very stiff, shaggy dough that just holds together when squeezed.
steps.mistake: Adding extra water because it seems dry, which makes soft, limp noodles.
steps.fix: Trust the measure; the dough will come together under pressure.

steps.do: Put the dough in a zip-lock bag, place it inside a second bag, wrap in a towel and rest for 30 minutes.
steps.look: The dough hydrates and becomes slightly more cohesive.
steps.mistake: Skipping the rest, making kneading harder.
steps.fix: Let the flour hydrate first.

steps.do: Lay the wrapped bags on the floor and, with clean socks on, step on the dough, flattening it with your heels into a disc about 12 inches (30 cm) across. Take it out, fold it in three, then roll into a ball. Repeat this stepping and folding 3 or 4 times.
steps.look: The dough becomes smooth, firm and elastic, with no cracks on the surface.
steps.mistake: Kneading by hand only, which is not strong enough for this stiff dough.
steps.fix: Use your weight; if cracks remain, keep going.

steps.do: Shape into a smooth ball, seal in the bag and rest at room temperature for 2 hours.
steps.look: A relaxed, smooth dough that rolls without springing back.
steps.mistake: Rolling too soon, so the dough shrinks back.
steps.fix: Rest longer.

steps.do: Simmer the aburaage in the dashi, soy, mirin and sugar for 10 to 15 minutes, turning, until most of the liquid is absorbed. Leave them in the syrup.
steps.look: Plump, glossy, amber pouches.
steps.mistake: Boiling hard, so the liquid evaporates before the tofu absorbs it.
steps.fix: Keep it at a gentle simmer.

steps.do: Dust the work surface with potato starch and roll the dough into a rectangle 1/8 inch (3 mm) thick, turning and dusting it often. Dust the top well, then fold it in thirds like a letter.
steps.look: An even, smooth sheet about 1/8 inch (3 mm) thick.
steps.mistake: Uneven thickness, so the noodles cook unevenly.
steps.fix: Roll from the centre outwards, checking thickness at the edges.

steps.do: Cut the folded dough across into strips 1/8 inch (3 to 4 mm) wide with the large knife, pushing straight down and forward. Shake the noodles out and toss with more starch.
steps.look: Long, square-edged noodles that do not stick together.
steps.mistake: Sawing with the knife, which squashes the noodles.
steps.fix: Use a single push down and forward, guided by the board's edge.

steps.do: Boil the noodles in plenty of unsalted water at a rolling boil for 10 to 12 minutes, stirring at first. Taste one: it should be chewy and cooked through. Drain and rinse vigorously in cold water to remove surface starch, then dip briefly in hot water to reheat.
steps.look: Glossy, slightly translucent, bouncy noodles.
steps.mistake: Salting the cooking water; the dough already holds salt.
steps.fix: Use unsalted water and taste the noodle for doneness.

steps.do: Heat the dashi with the soy, mirin and sugar to just below the boil. Place the noodles in warm bowls, ladle the hot broth over, and top with two pieces of tofu, kamaboko and spring onion. Serve with shichimi.
steps.look: Pale golden broth, white noodles and sweet amber tofu.
steps.mistake: Boiling the broth, which turns it cloudy and harsh.
steps.fix: Heat it gently, never boiling.

science: Udon owe their chew, koshi, to a firm, well-developed gluten network. The dough is very stiff, with about 45 percent water to flour, so kneading by hand is hard; stepping on it applies enough pressure to align the gluten. Salt is unusually high, about 5 percent of the flour, and it tightens the gluten so it is stronger and more elastic, and slows how quickly the noodles absorb water as they cook. Resting relaxes the gluten so the dough can be rolled thin. Rinsing after cooking washes off surface starch, making the noodles glossy rather than sticky. Dashi provides glutamates and inosinates from kombu and bonito, which together produce a strong savoury taste.
plating: Serve in deep, warm bowls. Lift the noodles in with chopsticks, folding them neatly. Pour the broth gently down the side to keep the noodles in place, then lay the two tofu pieces side by side on top with a slice or two of kamaboko and a small heap of spring onion. Shichimi on the table.

pairing.drink: A warm or chilled junmai sake, or hot roasted green tea (hojicha).

variations: Tanuki udon: top with crisp tempura batter bits instead of tofu.
Zaru udon: serve the noodles cold with a dipping sauce.
Curry udon: serve in a Japanese curry broth.
safety: Use a clean, food-safe bag, double bagged, when kneading by foot, and clean socks over clean feet.
A large pot of boiling water is heavy; lift the noodles out with a strainer rather than carrying the pot.
Use a sharp knife and a steady board, cutting with fingertips tucked back.

title: Jiaozi (Pork and Napa Cabbage Dumplings)
summary: Northern Chinese boiled dumplings with a juicy filling of hand-chopped pork and salted, squeezed napa cabbage, wrapped in home-made wrappers rolled thin at the edge and pleated shut. They teach salting vegetables to draw out water, rolling a wrapper thick in the middle and thin at the rim, and pleating a seal.
skills: a hot or cold water dough
equipment: Large mixing bowl and a pair of chopsticks
Clean tea towel or muslin for squeezing cabbage
Small Chinese rolling pin, a thin dowel about 1 inch (2.5 cm) thick
Sharp knife or bench scraper
Floured trays
Large pot of boiling water
Spider or slotted spoon
Instant-read thermometer

ingredients.item: Chinkiang black vinegar and chilli oil

mise: Make the dough first so it can rest (step 1).
Toss the chopped cabbage with its salt and leave 15 minutes.
Slice the spring onion and grate the ginger.
Flour two trays for the shaped dumplings.
Mix the dipping sauce: 3 parts black vinegar to 1 part soy, with slivered ginger and chilli oil.

timeline.do: Make the dough; rest 40 minutes.
Salt cabbage; wring dry; make filling; chill 30 minutes.
Roll wrappers and fill and pleat, about 40 dumplings.
Bring a large pot of water to the boil.
Boil in batches using the three cold-water additions.
Serve hot with dipping sauce.

steps.do: Stir the salt into the cold water, pour it into the flour and stir with chopsticks into a shaggy mass. Knead for 6 minutes until smooth. Cover and rest 40 minutes.
steps.look: A smooth, firm dough that springs back slowly and feels like an earlobe.
steps.mistake: A dough so soft and sticky that wrappers tear.
steps.fix: Knead in a little more flour; it should be firm.

steps.do: Gather the salted cabbage in the towel and wring it hard over the sink until no more water drips.
steps.look: A compact ball of cabbage less than half its original volume; a surprising amount of water comes out.
steps.mistake: Not squeezing hard enough, so the filling weeps and the dumplings split.
steps.fix: Squeeze in several goes.

steps.do: Put the pork in a bowl and beat in the cold stock in three additions, stirring hard in one direction with chopsticks for a minute after each, until the meat is sticky and holds together. Add the soy, wine, sesame oil, pepper, ginger, cabbage and spring onion and mix well. Chill 30 minutes.
steps.look: A sticky, glossy filling that holds a ridge.
steps.mistake: Adding the stock all at once, so it does not absorb and the filling is loose.
steps.fix: Add it gradually and beat between additions.

steps.do: Roll a quarter of the dough into a rope about 1 inch (2.5 cm) thick and cut into pieces of about 1/3 oz (10 g). Flatten each with your palm.
steps.look: Even little discs.
steps.mistake: Uneven pieces, so wrappers are different sizes.
steps.fix: Weigh the first few to learn the size.

steps.do: Roll each disc: hold the edge with one hand and roll the pin from the edge towards the centre and back, turning the disc a little after each stroke, to a round about 3 inches (8 cm) across.
steps.look: A wrapper thicker in the middle and thin at the edge.
steps.mistake: Rolling across the whole wrapper, so the middle is as thin as the edge and tears under the filling.
steps.fix: Roll only the outer edge, turning as you go.

steps.do: Place about 1/2 oz (15 g) of filling in the centre. Fold the wrapper in half and pinch the top middle. Make 3 or 4 small pleats on one side of the front edge, pressing each against the flat back edge, working from the middle towards each corner. Press firmly to seal.
steps.look: A crescent dumpling with pleats on one side and a tight seal.
steps.mistake: Wet or floury edges that will not stick.
steps.fix: Brush off excess flour, keep fingers dry, and dab the edge with water if needed.

steps.do: Set the dumplings on the floured tray, not touching. Bring a large pot of water to a rolling boil. Add 10 to 15 dumplings and stir gently so they do not stick. When the water returns to a hard boil, add 1 cup (240 ml) cold water. Repeat twice more.
steps.look: After the third return to the boil, the dumplings float, swell and the wrappers turn glossy and slightly translucent.
steps.mistake: Boiling hard non-stop, so wrappers tear before the filling cooks.
steps.fix: The cold-water additions cook the filling through gently.

steps.do: Check one: cut it open or probe the filling.
steps.look: The filling is firm and the centre reads 160°F (71°C).
steps.mistake: Undercooked pork in the centre.
steps.fix: Boil 1 to 2 minutes longer and recheck.

steps.do: Lift out with the spider and serve straight away with the dipping sauce.
steps.look: Plump, glossy dumplings, juicy inside.
steps.mistake: Letting them sit in a heap, where they stick.
steps.fix: Serve immediately, or toss with a few drops of sesame oil.

science: Cold water dough builds gluten slowly, giving an elastic wrapper strong enough to survive a rolling boil. Salt in the dough tightens the gluten further. Napa cabbage is mostly water; salting it draws water out of the cells by osmosis, so the filling does not release liquid inside the wrapper and burst the seam. Beating stock into the pork works because salt from the seasonings dissolves meat proteins called myosin, which become sticky and hold water, making a juicy, cohesive filling. Adding cold water during boiling brings the temperature down so the outside of the wrapper does not overcook before heat reaches the centre, and repeating it three times gives the filling time to reach a safe temperature.
plating: Arrange eight to ten dumplings on a warm plate in a neat circle, pleats facing up, or serve them in a bowl with a ladle of their cooking water as Northern families do. Set the dipping sauce in a small dish in the centre or beside each plate.

pairing.drink: A Tsingtao lager or an off-dry Riesling to balance the vinegar and chilli.

variations: Potstickers (guotie): fry the dumplings in oil until golden underneath, add water, cover and steam until it evaporates.
Pork and chive: replace the cabbage with chopped Chinese chives, unsalted.
Freeze ahead: freeze on a floured tray until solid, then bag, and boil from frozen, adding a minute.
safety: Pork fillings must reach 160°F (71°C) in the centre.
Keep the raw filling chilled while you shape, and wash hands, boards and knives after handling raw pork.

title: Empanadas Salteñas
summary: Argentine empanadas from Salta, with a lard pastry around a juicy filling of hand-cut beef, onion, spices, egg and olive, chilled firm, sealed with the repulgue rope crimp and baked hot. They combine pastry and dumpling skills: a chilled filling and a hand crimp.
skills: a juicy beef filling chilled firm
equipment: Large frying pan
Large mixing bowl
Rolling pin
4 inch (10 cm) round cutter or a saucer and knife
Two baking trays lined with baking paper
Pastry brush and a small bowl for egg wash
Sharp knife and board for hand-cutting beef
Instant-read thermometer

ingredients.note: with the salt dissolved in it

ingredients.item: Lard or oil for the filling

ingredients.note: optional, as many Salta cooks add

ingredients.item: Egg yolk beaten with 1 tbsp (15 ml) milk, for glazing

mise: Hand-cut the beef: slice it thin, cut into strips, then into small dice. Pat dry.
Chop the onions; slice the spring onion; boil, cool and chop the eggs; halve the olives.
Make the filling first so it can chill for at least 2 hours.
Line the trays with baking paper.

timeline.do: Cook the filling; spread out to cool; chill 2 hours.
Make the pastry; rest 30 minutes covered.
Roll and cut rounds; fill and crimp. Chill 15 minutes.
Heat the oven to 450°F (230°C).
Glaze and bake 12 to 15 minutes.
Rest 5 minutes and serve warm.

steps.do: Heat the lard in the frying pan over medium heat and cook the onions for 10 to 12 minutes until very soft and sweet but not browned. Add the cumin, paprika and chilli for 30 seconds.
steps.look: Soft, translucent onions coloured red by paprika.
steps.mistake: Browning the onions, which dries the filling.
steps.fix: Keep the heat medium-low; the onions provide the juice.

steps.do: Raise the heat, add the beef and salt and cook, stirring, for 3 to 4 minutes, until the beef has just lost its raw colour. Take off the heat and stir in the spring onion and potato if using.
steps.look: Beef just grey outside, still juicy, in a loose, juicy onion mixture.
steps.mistake: Cooking the beef fully, so it overcooks and dries in the oven.
steps.fix: Stop when the beef has just changed colour; it finishes cooking inside the pastry.

steps.do: Spread on a tray and refrigerate for at least 2 hours, until cold and the fat has set.
steps.look: A firm, cold filling with set fat.
steps.mistake: Filling empanadas with warm filling, which melts the pastry and bursts the seams.
steps.fix: Chill thoroughly; overnight is fine.

steps.do: For the pastry, put the flour in a bowl, pour in the warm melted lard and rub it in with your fingertips. Add the warm salted water gradually and knead for 3 to 4 minutes to a smooth, soft dough. Cover and rest 30 minutes.
steps.look: A soft, smooth, supple dough that does not stick.
steps.mistake: Overkneading, which makes a tough pastry.
steps.fix: Knead only until smooth.

steps.do: Roll the dough to 1/8 inch (3 mm) thick and cut 4 inch (10 cm) rounds. Gather and re-roll scraps once.
steps.look: About 12 even rounds.
steps.mistake: Rolling too thin, so the juicy filling tears through.
steps.fix: Keep an even 1/8 inch (3 mm).

steps.do: Place a heaped tablespoon of cold filling on each round with a piece of egg and an olive half. Brush the edge with water, fold in half and press firmly to seal, pushing out the air.
steps.look: Full half moons with no filling on the edges.
steps.mistake: Overfilling, so the edges will not meet.
steps.fix: Use a little less filling.

steps.do: Make the repulgue: starting at one corner, fold a small piece of the edge over itself, press, then fold the next piece over the first, working along the seam to form a rope pattern, about 12 folds.
steps.look: A neat, twisted rope along the curved edge.
steps.mistake: Loose folds that open in the oven.
steps.fix: Press each fold firmly; practise on the first few. A fork crimp works if the rope will not come.

steps.do: Chill the shaped empanadas for 15 minutes. Heat the oven to 450°F (230°C). Brush with egg wash and bake 12 to 15 minutes.
steps.look: Deep golden, glossy pastry, with juice just beginning to bubble at the seam. The filling reads 160°F (71°C).
steps.mistake: A low oven, so the pastry dries before it browns.
steps.fix: Use a fully heated hot oven.

steps.do: Rest 5 minutes and serve warm. Eat leaning forwards: they are juicy.
steps.look: Juice running out at the first bite.
steps.mistake: Biting straight from the oven.
steps.fix: Rest briefly; the inside is very hot.

science: The pastry uses warm melted lard rubbed into flour, which coats the flour proteins and limits gluten, giving a tender yet pliable dough that can be crimped without cracking. The filling is chilled so its fat sets solid and the juices are trapped in the jellied fat. In the hot oven the pastry sets and browns before the filling melts back into juice, so the juice stays inside rather than soaking the pastry and bursting the seam. Hand-cutting the beef keeps distinct pieces of meat that stay juicy, unlike mince. The egg yolk glaze browns fast through the Maillard reaction and gives shine.
plating: Arrange the empanadas on a wooden board or platter in a fan, crimped edges facing out to show the repulgue. Serve with a small bowl of llajua or chimichurri and lime wedges.

pairing.drink: A glass of Argentine Malbec or Torrontés; Malbec's ripe fruit and soft tannin match beef and spice.
pairing.brennans: Crawfish Meat Pies: Brennan's own hand pie, a good comparison for describing pastry, filling and crimp to guests.

variations: Fried empanadas: fry at 350°F (175°C) instead of baking.
Chicken empanadas: hand-cut chicken thigh with peppers.
Humita: a filling of creamed sweetcorn, onion and cheese.
safety: The beef filling must reach 160°F (71°C) in the centre.
Chill raw-meat filling promptly, and keep it in the fridge until shaping.
Juice inside is scalding; rest before biting.

title: Cornish Pasties
summary: A sturdy shortcrust wrapped around layers of raw beef skirt, potato, swede and onion with plenty of pepper, crimped along the side and baked slowly so the filling makes its own gravy. A shortcrust strong enough to hold a raw filling through a long bake is pastry's first real test.
skills: raw beef, potato, swede and onion layered
equipment: Large mixing bowl
Rolling pin
Dinner plate about 8 inches (20 cm) across, to cut rounds
Sharp knife and board
Baking tray lined with baking paper
Pastry brush
Cling film
Instant-read thermometer

ingredients.note: the higher protein makes a sturdy pastry
cut in small, thin pieces about 1/2 inch (1 cm), never minced
peeled, sliced thin and in small irregular pieces

ingredients.item: Fine salt and coarse black pepper for the filling

mise: Keep the lard and butter in the fridge until you use them.
Cut the beef into small, thin pieces with a sharp knife.
Peel the potato and swede and slice them thinly into small irregular pieces; keep potato in cold water if prepping ahead, then dry.
Chop the onion.
Heat the oven to 400°F (200°C) when the pastry is resting.

timeline.do: Make the pastry; rest 1 hour in the fridge.
Prepare the beef and vegetables.
Oven to 400°F (200°C). Roll, fill and crimp the pasties.
Bake 10 minutes at 400°F (200°C), then 40 to 45 minutes at 340°F (170°C).
Rest 15 minutes before serving.
Serve warm, eaten from the crimp end.

steps.do: Mix the flour and salt in the bowl. Rub in the cold lard and butter with your fingertips until it looks like coarse breadcrumbs with some pea-sized pieces of fat. Add the iced water gradually, mixing with a knife, until it comes together.
steps.look: A firm dough with small flecks of fat visible.
steps.mistake: Working the fat in until it melts, which makes a greasy, crumbly pastry.
steps.fix: Work fast with cold fingertips; chill the bowl for 10 minutes if it gets warm.

steps.do: Knead briefly for 1 to 2 minutes until smooth. This pastry needs a little more working than a tender tart pastry, to give strength. Wrap and chill 1 hour.
steps.look: A smooth, firm, pliable dough.
steps.mistake: Skipping the rest, so the pastry shrinks and tears.
steps.fix: Rest it fully.

steps.do: Divide the pastry into 4. Roll each piece to about 1/8 inch (3 to 4 mm) thick and cut a round about 8 inches (20 cm) across around the plate.
steps.look: Four even rounds.
steps.mistake: Rolling too thin, so the pastry tears with a raw, heavy filling.
steps.fix: Keep it at about 1/8 inch (3 to 4 mm).

steps.do: Layer the filling on one half of each round, leaving a 3/4 inch (2 cm) border: first potato and swede, seasoned with salt and pepper, then onion, then beef, seasoned again generously, then a little more potato. Top with a knob of butter.
steps.look: A neat, compact heap of raw filling.
steps.mistake: Overfilling so the edges will not meet.
steps.fix: Keep the filling compact and away from the edge.

steps.do: Brush the edge with water, fold the pastry over the filling and press the edges firmly together. Crimp the edge: starting at one end, fold the edge over itself and press, then repeat along the edge, making about 20 folds, so the crimp sits to one side.
steps.look: A D-shaped pasty with a thick, neat rope crimp along the curved side.
steps.mistake: Loose crimps that open, letting the juices escape.
steps.fix: Press each fold firmly.

steps.do: Place on the lined tray. Brush with beaten egg and cut a small steam hole in the top of each.
steps.look: Glossy pasties with a small vent.
steps.mistake: No steam hole, so the pastry splits.
steps.fix: Make a small slit with the tip of a knife.

steps.do: Bake at 400°F (200°C) for 10 minutes, then lower to 340°F (170°C) and bake 40 to 45 minutes more.
steps.look: Deep golden pastry; probe through the hole into the centre reads at least 160°F (71°C) and the potato is tender.
steps.mistake: Baking only at high heat, so the pastry burns before the raw filling cooks.
steps.fix: Follow the two temperatures; cover with foil if browning too fast.

steps.do: Rest the pasties for 15 minutes before eating.
steps.look: The filling settles and its juices thicken into a light gravy.
steps.mistake: Eating straight away; the filling is scalding.
steps.fix: Rest them; they are traditionally eaten warm, not hot.

science: A pasty needs a stronger crust than a tart. Strong bread flour has more protein, so a little kneading builds enough gluten for the pastry to hold a heavy, wet, raw filling for nearly an hour. The lard and butter, kept cold in small pieces, create layers that make the pastry short and flaky. The filling goes in raw and steams inside the sealed pastry: water from the vegetables and juices from the beef mix with the butter and starch from the potato into a light gravy. The first blast of high heat sets the pastry; the lower temperature then lets the filling cook through and the beef's connective tissue soften before the crust burns.
plating: Serve each pasty whole on a plate or a sheet of paper, crimp facing up. Some serve with brown sauce or a pickle, but the traditional pasty needs nothing at all.

pairing.drink: A dry farmhouse cider or a pint of bitter; both cut the rich pastry and peppery filling.

variations: Cheese and onion pasty: Cheddar, onion and potato for a vegetarian filling.
Steak and stilton: add crumbled blue cheese to the beef.
Mini pasties: cut 4 inch (10 cm) rounds and bake 30 minutes for party food.
safety: Raw beef filling must reach 160°F (71°C) in the centre; check through the steam hole.
Wash hands, knife and board after handling raw beef.
Cool leftovers quickly and reheat until steaming throughout.

title: Quiche Lorraine
summary: A crisp, blind-baked shortcrust shell filled with lardons and a rich egg and cream custard, baked until it is just set with a gentle tremble at the centre. It brings pastry and custard together: blind baking for a crisp base, and judging a custard by its wobble.
skills: a just-set bacon and egg custard
equipment: 9 inch (23 cm) loose-bottomed tart tin, at least 1 1/4 inches (3 cm) deep
Mixing bowl or food processor
Rolling pin
Baking paper and baking beans or dried beans
Baking tray
Frying pan for lardons
Jug and whisk
Instant-read thermometer

ingredients.note: or thick bacon cut in batons

ingredients.item: Double cream (or half cream, half whole milk)
Nutmeg, black pepper and a pinch of salt
ingredients.note: salt lightly; the lardons are salty
optional; the classic version has none

mise: Keep the butter cold.
Heat the oven to 400°F (200°C) with a baking tray inside while the pastry chills.
Cut a circle of baking paper larger than the tin, scrunch it up and smooth it out so it fits the corners.
Fry the lardons (step 6) while the shell bakes.
Grate the cheese if using.

timeline.do: Make the pastry; chill 30 minutes.
Roll and line the tin; chill 30 minutes.
Blind bake 15 minutes with beans, then 10 minutes without; seal with egg white.
Fry lardons; whisk the custard; oven to 325°F (160°C).
Fill and bake 30 to 40 minutes until barely trembling.
Cool at least 20 minutes, or to room temperature.
Slice and serve warm or at room temperature.

steps.do: Rub the cold butter into the flour and salt with your fingertips (or pulse in a food processor) until it looks like fine breadcrumbs. Mix the yolk with 2 tbsp (30 ml) iced water, add to the bowl and bring together with a knife, adding a little more water only if needed.
steps.look: A dough that just holds together when pressed, with no dry flour.
steps.mistake: Adding too much water, which makes a tough pastry that shrinks.
steps.fix: Add water a teaspoon at a time; stop as soon as it clumps.

steps.do: Flatten into a disc, wrap and chill 30 minutes. Roll on a floured surface to a round about 1/8 inch (3 mm) thick and 2 inches (5 cm) wider than the tin. Lift it over the rolling pin into the tin and press it into the corners without stretching it, leaving the excess hanging over the edge. Prick the base lightly with a fork. Chill 30 minutes.
steps.look: A smooth, even lining with pastry overhanging the rim.
steps.mistake: Stretching the pastry into the tin, which makes it shrink down the sides in the oven.
steps.fix: Lift and ease it into place; leave the overhang to trim after baking.

steps.do: Line the pastry with the scrunched baking paper and fill to the top with baking beans. Bake on the hot tray at 400°F (200°C) for 15 minutes.
steps.look: The edges are set and starting to colour.
steps.mistake: Too few beans, so the sides slump.
steps.fix: Fill right up to the rim, pressing beans into the corners.

steps.do: Lift out the paper and beans and bake for another 10 minutes until the base is dry and pale golden.
steps.look: A dry, sandy, pale gold base with no grey, raw-looking patches.
steps.mistake: Underbaking, which gives a soggy bottom under the wet custard.
steps.fix: Bake until golden; pale pastry never recovers once filled.

steps.do: Brush the hot base and sides with beaten egg white and return to the oven for 2 minutes. Trim the overhang with a sharp knife. Lower the oven to 325°F (160°C).
steps.look: A thin, glossy seal over the pastry.
steps.mistake: Cracks left open, where custard leaks underneath.
steps.fix: Patch cracks with a little leftover raw pastry before sealing.

steps.do: Fry the lardons in a dry pan over medium heat for 6 to 8 minutes until golden and the fat has rendered. Drain on kitchen paper.
steps.look: Golden, lightly crisp lardons.
steps.mistake: Adding greasy lardons, which leave oily pools in the custard.
steps.fix: Drain well.

steps.do: Whisk the eggs, yolks and cream in the jug until smooth but not frothy. Season with nutmeg, pepper and a little salt.
steps.look: A smooth, pale yellow custard.
steps.mistake: Whisking to a froth, which gives a bubbly, spongy top.
steps.fix: Whisk gently; skim off foam.

steps.do: Scatter the lardons (and cheese if using) in the shell. Set the tin on the tray in the oven, then pour the custard in to just below the rim.
steps.look: A shell filled almost to the top.
steps.mistake: Filling the tin on the counter, then spilling as you carry it.
steps.fix: Pour the last of the custard in with the tin already on the oven rack.

steps.do: Bake at 325°F (160°C) for 30 to 40 minutes, until the edges are set and lightly puffed, and the centre still trembles like jelly when you nudge the tin. The centre should read about 165 to 170°F (74 to 77°C).
steps.look: A golden, softly set custard with a gentle wobble in the middle 2 inches (5 cm).
steps.mistake: Baking until firm all over, so the custard turns rubbery and weeps.
steps.fix: Pull it while it trembles; it continues to set as it cools.

steps.do: Cool on a rack for at least 20 minutes before removing from the tin and slicing.
steps.look: A clean slice with a crisp base and silky custard.
steps.mistake: Slicing hot, so it collapses.
steps.fix: Let it cool and set.

science: Pâte brisée is tender because cold butter coats the flour, limiting gluten formation, and the small pieces of butter melt in the oven and leave flaky layers. Blind baking sets and dries the pastry before the wet custard goes in; otherwise the custard's moisture would soak into the raw dough. Egg white brushed on and baked forms a waterproof protein seal. The custard is a dilute mixture of egg proteins in cream: as it heats, the proteins unfold and link, trapping liquid in a soft gel. Below about 175°F (80°C) the gel stays silky; above it, the proteins tighten and squeeze out water, causing rubbery texture and weeping. A low oven and carryover heat give a just-set centre.
plating: Cut neat wedges with a sharp, warm knife, wiping it between cuts. Serve one wedge per plate, point towards the guest, with a green salad of soft leaves in a mustard vinaigrette alongside.

pairing.drink: An Alsace Pinot Gris or Riesling from just across the border from Lorraine; their richness and acidity match smoky bacon and cream.
pairing.brennans: Albert Boxler Pinot Gris 2020: a rich, textured Alsace Pinot Gris made for bacon, eggs and cream.

variations: Quiche aux poireaux: soften 2 sliced leeks in butter instead of lardons.
Spinach and goat's cheese: wilted, squeezed spinach and crumbled goat's cheese.
Mini quiches: use a muffin tin and bake for 15 to 18 minutes.
safety: Bake until the custard is set at the edges and just set at the centre, about 165 to 170°F (74 to 77°C).
Cool leftovers and refrigerate within 2 hours; eat within 3 days.

title: Pizza Margherita
summary: A thin, blistered pizza topped sparingly with crushed tomato, fresh mozzarella, basil and olive oil, on a dough that has fermented slowly in the fridge. It teaches hydration, cold fermentation, stretching by hand and the effect of the hottest heat a home oven can give.
equipment: Kitchen scale (essential for hydration)
Large mixing bowl and a dough scraper
Four small lidded containers or a tray with cling film
Baking steel or pizza stone
Pizza peel, or a rimless baking sheet
Semolina or flour for the peel
Instant-read or infrared thermometer (optional)
Pizza wheel or large knife

ingredients.item: Whole peeled San Marzano or plum tomatoes, canned

ingredients.note: torn and drained on kitchen paper for 30 minutes

mise: Weigh everything; dough hydration depends on exact quantities.
One to three days ahead, make the dough and put it in the fridge.
On the day, take the dough balls out 2 hours before baking.
Put the steel or stone on the top rack about 6 inches (15 cm) below the overhead grill (broiler) and heat the oven at its highest setting for at least 45 minutes.
Crush the tomatoes by hand with the salt into a rough sauce; do not cook it.
Tear and drain the mozzarella.

timeline.do: Mix the dough; rest 20 minutes; knead briefly; ball and refrigerate 24 to 72 hours.
Divide into 4 balls if not done; bring out to proof at room temperature 2 hours.
Oven and steel on at maximum.
Crush tomatoes; drain mozzarella; pick basil.
Stretch, top and bake each pizza 6 to 8 minutes.
Basil, oil, cut and serve one at a time.

steps.do: Mix the flour, yeast and water in the bowl until no dry flour remains. Cover and rest for 20 minutes. Add the salt and knead for 5 to 8 minutes, or use slap and folds on the counter, until the dough is smooth and elastic.
steps.look: A soft, slightly tacky dough that turns smooth and stretchy and passes the windowpane test.
steps.mistake: Adding flour because the dough feels sticky, which lowers the hydration and makes a dense crust.
steps.fix: Wet your hands or use a scraper rather than adding flour.

steps.do: Divide into 4 pieces of about 7 oz (205 g). Shape each into a tight ball by tucking the edges underneath and rolling it on the counter under a cupped hand. Put each in an oiled container or on an oiled tray, cover and refrigerate 24 to 72 hours.
steps.look: Smooth, taut balls.
steps.mistake: Loose balls, which spread flat and are hard to stretch evenly.
steps.fix: Reshape with more tension on the surface.

steps.do: Two hours before baking, take the dough out and leave it covered at room temperature to proof.
steps.look: The balls relax, puff, and feel soft and airy, with small bubbles visible under the surface.
steps.mistake: Stretching cold dough, which tears and springs back.
steps.fix: Give it the full time to warm and relax.

steps.do: Heat the oven with the steel at maximum, 500 to 550°F (260 to 290°C), for at least 45 minutes. Switch the grill on to high for the last 5 minutes before each pizza goes in.
steps.look: The steel is very hot; a sprinkle of flour on it browns within seconds.
steps.mistake: A steel that is not fully heated, so the base stays pale and soft.
steps.fix: Heat it for the full time.

steps.do: Flour a ball well, and press it from the centre outwards with your fingertips, leaving a 3/4 inch (2 cm) rim untouched. Lift it and stretch it over the backs of your hands, rotating, until it is about 10 inches (25 cm) across.
steps.look: A thin, even centre, nearly translucent, with a puffy rim.
steps.mistake: Using a rolling pin, which presses out the gas and leaves no rim.
steps.fix: Use fingertips and knuckles only.

steps.do: Lay the base on the peel dusted with semolina. Spread 3 tbsp (45 ml) of tomato thinly over it, leaving the rim bare. Scatter a quarter of the mozzarella, a few basil leaves and a drizzle of oil. Shake the peel to check the pizza slides.
steps.look: A sparse topping with plenty of red showing between the cheese.
steps.mistake: Overloading the pizza, which makes a soggy centre.
steps.fix: Less is more; a home oven cannot evaporate a lot of moisture.

steps.do: Slide the pizza onto the steel with a quick jerk of the peel. Bake 6 to 8 minutes, turning once halfway.
steps.look: The rim puffs and blisters with dark leopard spots; the cheese melts and bubbles; the base is crisp and spotted.
steps.mistake: A pizza that sticks to the peel and folds as it goes in.
steps.fix: Use more semolina and shake the peel before topping; work quickly once topped.

steps.do: Lift out with the peel, add fresh basil and a thread of olive oil, rest 1 minute, then cut and serve. Let the steel reheat for 5 minutes between pizzas.
steps.look: A glossy, bubbling pizza with charred spots on the rim.
steps.mistake: Cutting immediately, so the cheese slides off.
steps.fix: Rest briefly so the cheese sets slightly.

science: Hydration is the water as a percentage of the flour's weight; at 65 percent, the dough is soft enough to puff in the oven but manageable by hand. A long, cold fermentation slows yeast while enzymes break starch into sugars and proteins into flavour compounds, so the crust tastes richer and browns better. Cold also relaxes the gluten so the dough stretches easily. Stretching by hand keeps the gas bubbles in the rim, which expand dramatically in the heat. A baking steel stores and conducts heat fast, so the base crisps in minutes as water turns to steam and the surface browns through the Maillard reaction. Sparse toppings matter because every bit of water must boil away before the crust can crisp.
plating: Serve each pizza whole on a wooden board or a warm plate, uncut or cut into six. Add a few fresh basil leaves on top so they stay green, and finish with a thin thread of raw olive oil. Serve one pizza at a time, as they come out.

pairing.drink: A young Chianti Classico or a Barbera; their bright acidity matches tomato and cuts the mozzarella.
pairing.brennans: Fattoria di Fèlsina Chianti Classico 2022: a bright, savoury Sangiovese that matches tomato and basil.

variations: Marinara: tomato, garlic, oregano and olive oil, with no cheese.
Pizza bianca: olive oil, rosemary and sea salt on the base.
Same-day dough: double the yeast to 6 g and let it rise 2 hours at room temperature; less flavour, but it works.
safety: A steel or stone at 500 to 550°F (260 to 290°C) causes serious burns; use a peel and long oven gloves.
Keep a clear space in front of the oven when sliding pizzas in and out.
Let the steel cool in the oven for several hours before moving it.
